title: Requirements
body: Requirements What you need before installing. To put it together, go to Fast installation . What you need Computer Raspberry Pi 4 (this is what the rig was built and measured on) Surface Native Instruments Maschine MK2, over USB Audio Nothing extra required. The Pi's own headphone output works, and every figure in this project was measured on it at 48 kHz. An external interface Zynthian supports is optional and will sound better — but it is not what any of this was tested against Storage SD card, 16 GB or more — the ZynthianOS image is about 7.5 GB compressed Display Any HDMI monitor or TV for Zynthian's own UI, driven with a USB mouse and keyboard. A touchscreen is what the instrument was built around and is far nicer to play, but it is not required to install . You do need a screen eventually: saving snapshots happens there and nowhere else Network The Pi must reach the internet during installation

title: Fast installation
body: Fast installation Check the system requirements first — the hardware and the SD card matter, and nothing below works without them. Recommended. Six actions. About forty minutes, most of it unattended. At the end the instrument is running the factory snapshot: eight channels alive, the Maschine's pads lit in channel colours, both displays showing their tab rows, and a pattern playing the moment you press Play. Every step here is done by hand and explained in Manual installation . Come back to that page if something goes wrong, or if you would rather not run a script you have not read. 1 — Flash ZynthianOS Download the image and its checksum, verify it, then write it to the card with Raspberry Pi Imager. A truncated download produces a Pi that boots most of the way and then behaves inexplicably. curl -O https://os.zynthian.org/2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz curl -O https://os.zynthian.org/2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz.md5 md5sum -c 2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz.md5 # → 2026-01-27-zynthianos-oram-2601-stable.img.xz: OK Use this exact build. Newer vangelis images are a different, still-beta release train and nothing here has been tested on them. Give Raspberry Pi Imager the compressed file exactly as it downloaded. Do not unpack it first — Imager reads .img.xz as it is. In Imager choose Use custom , pick the file, pick the card, write. Zynthian's own walkthrough is Get the firmware . 2 — Boot the Pi The first boot is an initialisation pass, not a normal boot. Give it about half an hour and do not cut the power. ZynthianOS resizes its filesystem and configures itself the first time it comes up, and the touchscreen does not work reliably while that runs — a blank, frozen or garbled screen here is the install working, not a dead Pi. Everything below depends on this finishing, so let it finish. Upstream describes it as First Boot . Budget for the whole job: flashing and first boot about 30 minutes , the installer in step 5 about 10 minutes , so 40 minutes end to end, nearly all of it waiting. Card in, network cable in, power on. A display is optional — see below. ZynthianOS resizes its filesystem and starts its own UI. 3 — Find it on the network The install runs over SSH, so the Pi has to be reachable first. A cable straight from the Pi to your computer is enough; so is a switch. Boot the first time with a cable, or with a display. A fresh card holds no WiFi credentials and cannot be given any over WiFi — the admin menu needs a screen, webconf needs a network. Set the WiFi up once by either route, and the Pi is headless and cordless from then on. You have How to reach it A display The UI comes up on HDMI. Admin → Network Info shows the address No display Reach it by name: zynthian.local , or zynthian.lan . http://zynthian.local in a browser is webconf; ssh root@zynthian.local needs no address at all If neither name resolves, your machine is not doing mDNS — WSL2 never does. Take the Pi's address off your router; every URL and command here accepts it in place of the name. What Login webconf, in a browser password opensynth SSH user root , password opensynth — older images use raspberry Factory defaults, the same on every Zynthian. Change them in webconf before the instrument sits on a network you do not control. This is the step that traps newcomers — everything after it assumes the Pi answers. If it does not, Reaching the Pi in section 4 works through it at length: both ways out of the WiFi deadlock, the switch and direct-cable wiring, and what to do when the names do not resolve. Upstream's own tutorials are No Hardware Build and Accessing Zynthian from your computer . 4 — Log in over SSH ssh root@192.168.2.123 # substitute your own address # or, if the name resolves: ssh root@zynthian.local # password: opensynth # older images: raspberry As root , not as a user with sudo . That is how ZynthianOS is administered — the installer checks, and refuses to run as anyone else. 5 — Run one command curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Witzman/Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII/main/bootstrap.sh | bash This takes about ten minutes and looks like it has hung. It compiles the HID daemon on the Pi. Do not interrupt it. It ends by loading the factory snapshot and restarting Zynthian's UI, so the instrument is playing-ready when it returns. 6 — Press Play The snapshot is already loaded. The installer places it as Zynthian's default snapshot and restarts the UI, so the instrument comes up by itself on a fresh Pi. Nothing to tap. You should see this: Where What Touchscreen mixer eight strips plus main MK2 left display tab row A KICK , B SNAR , C CLAP , D CHAT MK2 right display tab row E OHAT , F BASS , G LEAD , H PADS MK2 Group buttons lit in channel colours MK2 mode buttons exactly one lit — CONTROL Nothing happened? What you see What it means What to do Pads dark, displays blank The daemon is not running systemctl status maschine-mk2 , then restart the daemon first and the UI second — the order matters Pads lit, but nothing responds The driver never bound to the daemon's port Re-run the installer; it re-applies the zynautoconnect patch A tab is dashed That channel is silent on purpose — muted, or its generator is set to never fire Not a fault. The dashed tab is the instrument's way of explaining silence Zynthian came up empty, no mixer strips This Pi had a previous session. Zynthian restores its last state before falling back to the factory default Load it by hand: Snapshots → into bank 000 → 017-generative-techno . From the screen, or from webconf's Snapshots page Anything else: work through Manual installation , which gives each step's own check.

title: Features
body: Features An eight-channel generative groovebox on Zynthian, played entirely from a Native Instruments Maschine MK2 — pads, encoders, both displays, LEDs. Five euclidean drum channels and three Turing-machine voices, all eight always alive; nothing is created or torn down while playing. The generator owns the pattern. You do not draw a beat. You set hits, rotation and randomness, and the driver writes real notes into Zynthian's own sequencer — so patterns persist in snapshots and the touchscreen pattern editor mirrors exactly what the pads show. How to play it starts at Quick start ; how it is built is Internals . The eight channels Group Name Kind Engine MIDI ch Colour A KICK drum LinuxSampler, an SFZ drum machine 1 red B SNAR drum LinuxSampler 2 orange C CLAP drum LinuxSampler 3 amber D CHAT drum LinuxSampler 4 yellow-green E OHAT drum LinuxSampler 5 green F BASS voice JC303 6 blue G LEAD voice Obxd 7 violet H PADS voice padthv1 8 cyan Drums are warm colours and voices cool, so the seam between the halves is visible on the panel without reading anything. All eight are always alive — nothing is created or torn down while playing. The factory snapshot ships one channel against that grain. E · OHAT keeps its Simmons kit and its sampler, but arrives switched to voice behaviour: the Turing register walks the kit's own samples rather than euclid placing them. It is there so the switch below is audible the moment you plug in. Its tab reads VOX , and GRID blinks while it is selected. What it does Each of these has a page with a walkthrough on the real instrument. Generating patterns Euclidean drums and Turing-machine voices. You set hits, rotation and randomness; the generator writes the notes and you steer it. Playing and recording The pads are the instrument. Hold REC and what you play is captured into the same pattern the generator writes — and the pattern becomes yours. Modulation Hold MOD and every encoder stops setting a value and starts setting how that value moves. Saved with the set, still running tomorrow. Sound and presets Kits, samples and engine presets, changed while the rig plays — and switching what a channel behaves as without swapping its engine. Deep parameter control Eight knobs reaching a synth's fortieth parameter, on pages built from whatever the plugin publishes — and the eight buttons above them carrying that plugin's switches by name. Mixing and effects One control across all eight channels, two post-fader inserts on every one, and the globals that belong to the machine. The surface Every button, both displays, what each light means, and the list to work down when a channel goes quiet — plus the phrase clock and ARM, which land a change on a bar you choose instead of the moment you press. Saving your work What a snapshot carries, what it cannot, and the one control in the web interface that looks like a save button and is not. What it is not No song mode, no pattern chaining, no sampling, no audio recording. Eight channels, always alive. It is an instrument for playing a single evolving pattern, not a workstation for arranging one.

title: Quick start
body: Quick start Two minutes from a running rig to something worth listening to. Everything here is reversible and nothing needs saving to keep playing. Your first two minutes Press Play . All eight channels start together, and the factory snapshot already holds a beat and three voices. Press Group A to select KICK, then STEP . Encoder 1 is HITS: turn it to 4 and you have four-on-the-floor. Encoder 2 is ROTATE — turn it and the same four hits slide around the bar without changing how many there are. Press Group F for BASS, still in STEP. Encoder 3 is MELODY. Turn it to roughly 30 and the bassline starts mutating a note at a time. When a phrase goes past that you want, turn MELODY back to 0: the cell reads LOCK and that line is now frozen, bit for bit, until you move the knob again. Press CONTROL and the same eight encoders become what the channel sounds like instead of what it plays. That is the whole instrument in miniature — a mode decides what the knobs mean, the channel decides what they act on. Nothing you have touched is destructive, and nothing needs saving to keep playing. When you do want to keep it, see Saving a set . Where next Every feature has a page with a walkthrough like the one above — the full list is on Features . The three worth reading first: Generating patterns — euclid, the Turing register, and what LOCK really means Modulation — making any sound parameter move on its own The surface — every button, and what to check when a channel goes quiet

body: Manual installation This is what bootstrap.sh does, step by step, for readers installing by hand or debugging an install that went wrong. Every step states what it does, why it is needed, and how to confirm it worked. This page starts from a Pi that already runs ZynthianOS. Flashing the card is not part of the install — it happens before any of it, and it is the same for both routes: step 1 of Fast installation has the image, the checksum and how to write it, and Zynthian's own walkthrough is Get the firmware . The first boot is an initialisation pass, not a normal boot. Give it about half an hour and do not cut the power. ZynthianOS resizes its filesystem and configures itself the first time it comes up, and the touchscreen does not work reliably while that runs — a blank, frozen or garbled screen here is the install working, not a dead Pi. Nothing below can be reached until it finishes. Upstream describes it as First Boot . Run everything on the Pi, as root , from the repository root. ZynthianOS is administered as root, and root SSH login is enabled out of the box. There is also a zynthian user in the sudo group, but nothing here uses it — bootstrap.sh refuses to run below uid 0, and the steps below assume root: ssh root@zynthian.local # or the IP; password: opensynth, older images raspberry git clone https://github.com/Witzman/Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII cd Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII Reaching the Pi Everything below is typed on the Pi over SSH, so start by getting there. An ethernet cable straight from the Pi to your computer works, and so does a switch. Plan on a cable or a display for the first contact — WiFi cannot be set up over WiFi. A freshly flashed card holds no WiFi credentials, and every way of giving it some needs the Pi already reachable: the admin menu needs a screen, webconf and VNC need a network. Boot a fresh card with no cable and it joins nothing, with no way in. The hotspot has the same catch — it is switched on from the admin menu, so it is a convenience once you are in, not a way of getting in. Way out of it What you do Display, once Attach HDMI, set the WiFi up in the UI's admin menu, unplug the display. It never needs to come back Cable, once Boot with ethernet, take the address, reach webconf or VNC, set the WiFi up there, unplug the cable Either one is a one-off. After it the Pi comes up on WiFi by itself and the rig is headless for good. Route How Display attached The UI comes up on HDMI. Admin → Network Info shows the address. It also appears on the error screen No display ssh root@zynthian.local , or http://zynthian.local for webconf. zynthian.lan is the same machine under a second name Neither name resolves Your side is not doing mDNS. Some systems need it enabled; WSL2 never resolves .local . Take the address from your router and use it in place of the name What Login webconf password opensynth SSH user root , password opensynth . Older images use raspberry These are factory defaults, identical on every Zynthian. Change them in webconf before the instrument sits on a network you do not control. None of this is ours — it is stock Zynthian, and the project's own wiki is the place to go when a route here does not fit your setup. No Hardware Build covers flashing, first boot and the network from scratch; Accessing Zynthian from your computer is the fuller list of ways in — VNC, SFTP, WiFi hotspot, and the Windows and macOS notes. Before you start Confirm the machine is what the rest of this page assumes. Check Command Expected OS build head -1 /zynthian/build_info.txt contains Oram-2601-1 UI branch git -C /zynthian/zynthian-ui branch --show-current oram-2601.1 webconf open http://<pi> the configuration page loads A different branch means another release train. Nothing here has been run on vangelis , which is still beta. The daemon and the driver Step 1 — Build the daemon What. Compiles the Rust HID daemon that speaks to the Maschine. Why. No binary is shipped; the daemon is built where it runs. How to confirm. daemon/target/release/maschine exists and is executable. apt install -y rustc cargo cd daemon && cargo build --release && cp picturetest.png target/release/ && cd .. Minutes on a Pi 4. Do not interrupt it. Step 2 — Put the daemon config in place What. Installs pad note offsets, encoder CC numbers, and external_pad_leds . Why. Without "external_pad_leds": true the daemon repaints the pads itself in its own global colour, and the first pad you touch destroys the driver's per-channel picture. How to confirm. The grep prints the flag as true . cp system/maschine.json daemon/maschine.json grep external_pad_leds daemon/maschine.json # → "external_pad_leds": true Step 3 — Install the udev rule What. Creates the stable /dev/maschine symlink and restarts the daemon on replug. Why. Otherwise the daemon must be pointed at a /dev/hidrawN number that moves between boots. How to confirm. /dev/maschine exists and points at a hidraw node. install -m 0644 system/99-maschine.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/99-maschine.rules udevadm control --reload-rules udevadm trigger --subsystem-match=hidraw Step 4 — Install the helper scripts What. Puts the JACK connect and clock helpers in /usr/local/bin . Why. maschine-jack-connect.sh sets the port alias virtual:maschine.rs/Maschine MK2 Pads . Zynthian derives a control-device id from the part of an alias after the first / , and a2j gives user-client ports no alias at all — without it the driver has no id to bind to and never loads. How to confirm. All three files are present and executable. install -m 0755 system/maschine-jack-connect.sh /usr/local/bin/ install -m 0755 system/maschine-clock-bridge.py /usr/local/bin/ install -m 0755 system/maschine-clock-connect.sh /usr/local/bin/ Step 5 — Install and enable the systemd units What. Installs the daemon, its web editor and the clock bridge as services. Why. The daemon must survive reboots and reconnect to JACK by itself. How to confirm. systemctl is-active maschine-mk2 prints active , and the MK2's displays light. install -m 0644 system/maschine-mk2.service /etc/systemd/system/ install -m 0644 system/maschine-web.service /etc/systemd/system/ install -m 0644 system/maschine-clock.service /etc/systemd/system/ systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable --now maschine-mk2 maschine-web maschine-clock If you cloned anywhere other than /root/Generative-Techno-ZynthianMaschine-MKII , edit ExecStart and WorkingDirectory in maschine-mk2.service , and --directory in maschine-web.service . install.sh rewrites these for you; by hand it is on you. Step 6 — Let a2jmidid export software clients What. Makes the daemon's ALSA sequencer port visible in JACK. Why. Without a JACK port, step 4's script has nothing to connect or alias. How to confirm. The port appears. jack_lsp | grep "Pads MIDI" # → a2j:maschine rs [N] (playback): Maschine MK2 Pads MIDI Step 7 — Patch zynautoconnect What. The only change to a Zynthian core file: adds the Pads port to the hardware-MIDI-source whitelist so it gets a zmip slot, and pins the stable uid. Why. Without it the driver never binds and the rig does nothing, with no error in any log — the most confusing failure in this project. Internally Zynthian gets as far as Found and never reaches Loaded , but both are INFO messages you will not see at the default log level; see step 10. How to confirm. The grep returns 1 or more. python3 tools/patch-autoconnect-maschine.py grep -c "maschine rs.*Pads MIDI" /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zynautoconnect/zynthian_autoconnect.py It ships as a patcher rather than a copy, so it edits your file. It is idempotent. Re-run it after every Zynthian system update — an update replaces zynthian_autoconnect.py and takes the binding with it. Step 8 — Copy the three driver files What. Drops the control-surface driver into Zynthian's ctrldev directory. Why. Two traps. These are untracked drop-ins in a checkout that tracks upstream, so never use git in /zynthian/zynthian-ui — a git reset --hard deletes them and the running instrument with them. And every module there needs a dev_ids attribute; without it the whole UI crash-loops every 14 seconds. How to confirm. All three files are present in the target directory. install -m 0644 ctrldev/zynthian_ctrldev_maschine_mk2.py \ ctrldev/techno_lib.py \ ctrldev/maschine_mk2_lib.py \ /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngine/ctrldev/ Step 9 — Restart, daemon first and UI second What. Brings both halves up in the one order that works. Why. Restarting the daemon alone makes a2j re-register the Pads port onto a new zmip slot while the driver stays bound to the dead one. The rig goes silent, no error appears anywhere, and a stale route is left behind that makes every later pad tap fire twice. How to confirm. Zynthian's UI comes back on the display. systemctl restart maschine-mk2 sleep 8 systemctl restart zynthian Step 10 — Confirm the surface is alive What. Proves the driver bound and the routing is clean. Why. No route means step 7 did not take effect; two routes mean a stale one from an earlier session is still alive, and every pad tap will fire twice. How to confirm. Exactly one ZynMidiRouter:devN_in under the Pads port. jack_lsp -c | awk '/\(capture\): Pads MIDI/{f=1;next} /^[^ \t]/{f=0} f{print}' # → ZynMidiRouter:dev2_in ← exactly one line, and nothing else Do not expect a particular slot number. Patched Zynthian assigns the slot itself, and it varies; this rig runs on dev2_in . Nothing else may connect that port — a second connector is what produced a duplicate route here, and two routes make every pad tap fire twice. See Why there is no "Loaded" line below before hunting through the journal. Why not grep -A3 . The obvious form of this check, jack_lsp -c | grep -A3 "Pads MIDI" , reports a healthy rig as a broken one. It matches the Pads port twice — once as a port and once as another port's connection — and the three lines it then prints are unrelated ports sitting at the left margin: a2j:maschine rs [129] (capture): Pads MIDI ZynMidiRouter:dev2_in ← the only real route a2j:maschine rs [129] (playback): MIDI Control ttymidi:MIDI_in -- a2j:maschine rs [129] (capture): Pads MIDI ZynMidiRouter:dev3_in ← these three are ports, not routes ZynMidiRouter:dev4_in ZynMidiRouter:dev5_in Four devN_in lines, one actual route. Read that as a fault and the fix you would reach for — disconnecting the "extras" — breaks a rig that was working. Indentation is the whole distinction: a route is indented under its port, a port starts at the left margin. The awk form above prints only the indented lines belonging to the Pads capture port, so it cannot mislead. With no snapshot loaded the MK2 draws both tab rows, the Group buttons in channel colours, and the CONTROL button lit. Nothing sounds yet — no chains exist. Plugins and drum kits Step 11 — Install the packaged plugins What. Installs three of the five engines from Debian. Why. obxd-lv2 is channel G, padthv1-lv2 is channel H, and tap-lv2 provides TAP Reverberator and TAP Stereo Echo for all sixteen inserts. How to confirm. Three Status: install ok installed lines. apt install -y obxd-lv2 padthv1-lv2 tap-lv2 dpkg -s obxd-lv2 padthv1-lv2 tap-lv2 | grep ^Status Step 12 — Confirm JC303 What. Checks the bass engine, which is not a Debian package. Why. It comes from Zynthian's own plugin set; if missing, install it through webconf so the plugin cache learns about it. How to confirm. The directory exists. ls -d /zynthian/zynthian-plugins/lv2/JC303.lv2 Step 13 — Enable the plugins and regenerate the LV2 cache What. In webconf: Engines , enable Obxd, padthv1, JC303, TAP Reverberator and TAP Stereo Echo, then Regenerate LV2 Cache . Why. A plugin that is installed but not enabled is invisible to a snapshot, and loading one that names a disabled plugin gives a chain with no engine. How to confirm. All five appear as available engines. Let the scan finish before loading anything. Step 14 — Confirm the SFZ drum kits What. Checks the kits the five drum channels play. Why. Missing kits load silently — the channels exist and make no sound. Use find -type f : one entry is a directory , so ls over-counts. How to confirm. A count greater than zero. find "/zynthian/zynthian-data/soundfonts/sfz/Drum Machines" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.sfz' | wc -l # → 40 (on the rig this was written from) The snapshot Step 15 — Copy it into a bank What. Places the factory snapshot in bank 000 . Why. The bank subdirectory is not optional — a snapshot at the snapshots root is invisible in the UI. How to confirm. The file is listed under 000/ . install -m 0644 snapshot/017-generative-techno.zss \ /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/000/ Step 16 — Make it the default, so it loads by itself What. Copies the same file to the snapshots root as default.zss . Why. At startup Zynthian restores last_state.zss if there is one, and otherwise falls back to default.zss — which is exactly the fresh-install case, so the instrument comes up without anyone touching a screen. default.zss is only ever written by an explicit save as default , so seeding it destroys nothing, and a Pi with an existing session keeps its own. How to confirm. Restart the UI; it comes up in the mixer, not the main menu. install -m 0644 snapshot/017-generative-techno.zss \ /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/default.zss systemctl restart zynthian Step 17 — Or load it by hand What. Opens Snapshots, goes into bank 000 , taps 017-generative-techno . Why. Needed only if this Pi already had a session, whose last_state.zss takes priority over the default. Loading takes about fifteen seconds: eight engines start, sixteen plugin hosts come up, and the driver re-reads its parameters out of the sequencer. How to confirm. Eight mixer strips plus main, both tab rows drawn. Never save from webconf's Snapshots page. Its Name: field plus the checkmark renames the selected bank — it has destroyed bank 000 here once. Loading from webconf is safe; saving from it is not. Step 18 — The genre pack What. Places fifty more snapshots, 031 – 080 , in the same bank. Why. They are fixed arrangements to start from — ten each of house, deep house, minimal, dub and trance — and unlike the factory snapshot they are optional : the instrument is complete without them. They are not copied over default.zss , because the factory snapshot is what a fresh Pi should boot into. How to confirm. Fifty files listed under 000/ . install -m 0644 snapshot/genre-pack/*.zss \ /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/000/ find /zynthian/zynthian-my-data/snapshots/000 -name '0[3-8][0-9]-*.zss' | wc -l # → 50 bootstrap.sh does this for you; this step is for a hand install. Every voice in the pack arrives at LOCK with no modulation, so a preset plays the same bar until you turn something. Notes You do not need a touchscreen The UI is ordinary HDMI: a monitor or TV with a USB mouse and keyboard drives it, and webconf's Snapshots page loads a snapshot from a browser with no screen attached at all. A touchscreen is what the instrument was built around and is far nicer to play — but the rig runs headless, and only saving a snapshot needs the UI itself. Which does not have to be a physical screen. Zynthian ships a VNC server — webconf, INTERFACE → UI Options → Enable VNC Server — and the whole UI then runs in a browser at http://zynthian.local:6080/vnc.html , with the engines' own desktop on :6081 . Confirmed working on this rig. That is the headless answer for anything the UI owns, snapshot saving included: a Pi with no display, no keyboard and no mouse is still fully driveable from the computer you installed from. Why there is no "Loaded" line Zynthian logs Found ctrldev driver … and Loaded ctrldev driver … at INFO , while ZYNTHIAN_LOG_LEVEL defaults to WARNING (30). On a stock rig neither line is ever written, whether the driver loaded or not, so their absence proves nothing — the JACK route in step 10 is the check that works as shipped. To see them, uncomment the line Zynthian ships for it in /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zynthian.sh , set it to 20, and restart the UI: export ZYNTHIAN_LOG_LEVEL=20 # 10=DEBUG, 20=INFO, 30=WARNING (the default) systemctl restart zynthian Measured, not assumed: at level 20 the two lines appear as INFO:zynthian_ctrldev_manager.update_available_drivers: Found ctrldev driver 'zynthian_ctrldev_maschine_mk2' for devices with ID 'Maschine MK2 Pads' INFO:zynthian_ctrldev_manager.load_driver: Loaded ctrldev driver 'Maschine MK2 Drum Rig' for 'Maschine MK2 Pads'. Note what the Loaded line is keyed on. It carries the driver's display name, Maschine MK2 Drum Rig — not the module name. A grep for maschine_mk2 finds the Found line and misses the Loaded one, which is the one that matters. Grep for ctrldev driver instead. zynthian.sh is a core Zynthian file, so a system update reverts it. There is no setting for this in webconf. Verify bash tools/check-prereqs.sh; echo "exit=$?" # → exit=0 once loaded jack_lsp | grep -c TAP # → 64 cd ctrldev && python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -q # → Ran 271 tests … OK The unit tests run anywhere — no Pi, no Maschine. They are the only automated proof this project has: the driver cannot be imported off the Pi, so everything generative and presentational lives in techno_lib.py , which has no Zynthian imports and is tested. When it does not work Symptom Cause Fix Displays blank, buttons dark, Zynthian fine daemon not running systemctl status maschine-mk2 , then journalctl -u maschine-mk2 -n 50 Surface dead, no devN_in under the Pads port no zmip slot — the driver never bound Step 7, then restart daemon and UI No Pads MIDI in jack_lsp a2jmidid not exporting software clients Step 6 Every pad tap fires twice a stale JACK route Step 10, using the awk form — only an indented second devN_in is a real duplicate. Repair by restarting the daemon, then the UI Whole UI restarts every ~14 s a module in ctrldev/ without dev_ids Step 8 First pad touch destroys the pad colours external_pad_leds missing Step 2, then restart the daemon and the UI Input dies after seconds, then recovers kernel hidraw fault; the daemon reopens the device Nothing to do. watchdog: input stalled, reopened about every 8 s is healthy A channel is silent, tab dashed muted, or its generator is silent — HITS 0, or play chance 0 Not a fault. title: Internals

headings.text: Why zynautoconnect has to be patched
The insert pair, measured on the wire
Sixteen inserts without placing sixteen processors

body: Internals How the instrument is built. What it does is Features ; how to install it is Manual installation . The control path A pad press reaches the sequencer through five hops, and every one of them has broken at least once: flowchart LR HID["Maschine MK2 USB HID"] --> D["maschine daemon Rust"] D --> A["a2jmidid virtual port"] A --> Z["ZynMidiRouter zmip slot"] Z --> C["ctrldev driver Python"] C --> S["zynseq Zynthian's sequencer"] The daemon owns the hardware: it reads HID reports, drives both 255×64 displays and the LEDs, and exposes an ALSA sequencer port. a2jmidid lifts that port into JACK. Zynthian then has to be persuaded to treat it as a hardware MIDI source so it is given a zmip slot — and that is the patch below. Encoders are relative. The daemon holds each encoder's value as device state and moves it by the hardware delta. Real movement is 0-4 units per report and a counter wrap reads as −38 to −40, so the wrap guard is 8. The big encoder sends 8 units per detent and wraps 120 → 0, sitting exactly on that threshold, so it needs its own delta path. Why zynautoconnect has to be patched It is the only Zynthian core file this project changes, and it ships as an idempotent patcher rather than a copy, so it edits your version instead of overwriting it. Two changes. The Pads port joins the list of ports treated as hardware MIDI sources, which is what earns it a zmip slot. And the uid virtual:maschine.rs/Maschine MK2 Pads is pinned, because the ALSA client number embedded in the port name changes across boots while a ctrldev driver binds by device id. Unpatched, the driver never binds: Zynthian gets as far as Found and never reaches Loaded . The rig does nothing, and no log anywhere says why — literally, because both of those messages are logged at INFO while ZYNTHIAN_LOG_LEVEL defaults to WARNING, so neither is written on a stock rig. The check that works is the JACK route: exactly one ZynMidiRouter:devN_in under the Pads port. Re-run the patcher after every Zynthian update: an update replaces the file and takes the binding with it. The driver The generator owns the pattern. The driver does not synthesise notes at play time — it writes them into zynseq, which is why patterns survive in snapshots and why the touchscreen editor shows the same thing the pads do. Playing is Zynthian's job; the driver only decides what is written. Three facts hold the design together. Everything testable lives outside the driver. The driver itself cannot be imported off the Pi — it needs zynlibs.zynseq — so the Turing register and its mutation, the undo ring, register-to-pitch quantisation, euclidean placement, the gate mask, and the whole page and column model were pushed into techno_lib.py , which has no Zynthian imports. That module carries its own test suite, including the invariant the instrument rests on: a generator at LOCK produces a byte-identical register over 500 iterations — which now has to hold for the rhythm register as well as the pitch one. Every zynseq call holds one lock. libzynseq is not thread-safe and the driver reaches it from three threads — the MIDI handler, a queued signal handler and a 30 Hz playhead poll. Without the lock the entire Zynthian UI died with a segfault about 95 seconds into a jam. Nothing slow runs on the MIDI thread. Loading a preset blocks on a socket for seconds while the MIDI handler holds the lock for the whole event, so preset and kit changes are deferred to the poll thread. A silent channel must say why. Play chance 0 emits nothing and looked exactly like a hang, so a channel that cannot sound draws its tab dashed. It is the one mechanism the surface has for explaining silence. The factory snapshot The eight chains Chain Title in the snapshot Engine MIDI channel (0-based in the file) A Kick LS/LinuxSampler 0 B Snare LS/LinuxSampler 1 C Clap LS/LinuxSampler 2 D Closed Hat LS/LinuxSampler 3 E Open Hat LS/LinuxSampler 4 F BASS JV/JC303 5 G LEAD JV/Obxd 6 H PADS JV/padthv1 7 The MIDI channel is the contract , not the title and not the order — the driver resolves a channel to a chain by MIDI channel, so titles are free and numbers are not. All five drum chains share one LinuxSampler process, so eight SFZ kits cost about 250 MB in total rather than per channel. The insert pair, measured on the wire zynmixer:output_NNa/b → TAP_Stereo_Echo-NN → TAP_Reverberator-NN → zynmixer:input_17 Echo first, reverb second, so the reverb hears the echo's repeats. The order was read out of jack_lsp -c on the running rig, not assumed. The inserts are fed from the strip's output , which is what makes them post-fader: they inherit the fader and the mute, so muting a channel takes its reverb and delay tail with it. Both plugins have a true wet level, not a dry/wet crossfade — sweep the wet to maximum and the dry is still there at the same level. That is what lets encoders 7 and 8 behave like sends. Every cheaper candidate measured turned out to be a crossfade. Four ports are forced rather than left at their defaults: Plugin Port Value Why TAP Stereo Echo dryLevel 0.0 dB Ships at −4 dB; across the pair that quietly costs every channel about 8 dB TAP Stereo Echo lecholevel , recholevel −70.0 dB Wet starts closed; encoder 8 opens it TAP Reverberator drylevel 0.0 dB Same reason TAP Reverberator wetlevel −70.0 dB Wet starts closed; encoder 7 opens it Gain staging Channel strips 0.19 , main 0.80 . That is measurement, not caution: one sampler channel peaks at 1.24 before the mixer, and eight summed to 2.92 on the main bus — nearly three times full scale. The sampler's own volume is not the lever; taking it from 96 to 40 moved the bus peak by about 1.5 dB. Sixteen inserts without placing sixteen processors Build one channel by hand on the touchscreen — add TAP Stereo Echo, then TAP Reverberator, set the four values, save — and let tools/build-techno-snapshot.py replicate it. The cloner finds the chain carrying both inserts, appends the same two to every other chain that has a MIDI channel, gives each a fresh processor id, copies the template's fader position, and backs the file up first. Then load and save once more from the touchscreen, so what is on disk is Zynthian's own output rather than the script's. It deliberately does not build the whole snapshot. Nothing outside the UI process can reach Zynthian's live state manager, and hand-maintaining fader positions in JSON is exactly the kind of guess this project avoids. title: Touchscreen patch
body: Touchscreen patch Optional. Not part of the instrument. Apply it only if you have the symptom below. Who needs this Your touchscreen reports touches at the wrong place — usually compressed into one corner or scaled toward one edge — while the same screen displays correctly. That happens when the panel's touch controller reports coordinates in its own native resolution while Zynthian's UI is running at a different configured display size. Zynthian passes the raw touch value straight through, so a panel reporting 0-4095 on a 800×480 UI puts every touch in the top-left eighth of the screen. This was the case on the rig this guide was written from: an Elecrow 5" 800×480 panel, HDMI for video and USB for touch. If your touch already lands where you press, skip this page. The patch edits a Zynthian core file, and there is no reason to carry a change you do not need. The patch It scales the raw touch value onto Zynthian's configured display size, guarding against a zero maximum so an unreported range cannot divide by zero. File: /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py , in MultiTouch 's evdev event loop. @@ class MultiTouch(object): elif evdev_event.code == ecodes.ABS_MT_POSITION_X: - if self._invert_x: - self._current_touch.x_root = self.max_x - evdev_event.value - else: - self._current_touch.x_root = evdev_event.value + raw = self.max_x - evdev_event.value if self._invert_x else evdev_event.value + self._current_touch.x_root = int(raw * zynthian_gui_config.display_width / self.max_x) if self.max_x else raw if self._current_touch not in self.events: self.events.append(self._current_touch) elif evdev_event.code == ecodes.ABS_MT_POSITION_Y: - if self._invert_y: - self._current_touch.y_root = self.max_y - evdev_event.value - else: - self._current_touch.y_root = evdev_event.value + raw = self.max_y - evdev_event.value if self._invert_y else evdev_event.value + self._current_touch.y_root = int(raw * zynthian_gui_config.display_height / self.max_y) if self.max_y else raw if self._current_touch not in self.events: self.events.append(self._current_touch) Both hunks keep the existing _invert_x / _invert_y handling and only add the scaling on top of it. Applying it Back the file up first — this is a Zynthian core file, not one of ours. ssh root@<pi> cp /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py \ /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py.bak # edit the two handlers as shown above systemctl restart zynthian Verify: press each corner of the screen and confirm the UI responds at that corner. To undo it: cp /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py.bak \ /zynthian/zynthian-ui/zyngui/multitouch.py systemctl restart zynthian Two warnings A Zynthian update overwrites it. multitouch.py is tracked in the zynthian-ui checkout, so any update replaces your edit. Keep the .bak , and expect to re-apply after upgrading. Do not run git checkout or git reset in /zynthian/zynthian-ui to undo this. That directory also holds this project's three driver files as untracked drop-ins; a hard reset removes the instrument along with the patch. Restore from the .bak copy instead. title: Deep parameter control

headings.text: Switches: the eight buttons above the knobs
What this costs, and where mute went

body: Deep parameter control Eight knobs, and a synth with forty parameters. This is how you reach the fortieth without a menu. What it is Page 1 of CONTROL gives a voice the four controls anyone reaches for first — CUTOFF, RESO, ENV, DECAY. Everything else the plugin publishes fills further CONTROL pages , eight ports to a page, in the plugin's own order and under the plugin's own names. Nothing in the driver knows what those parameters are. It asks the plugin what it has and builds the pages from the answer, which is why a synth nobody planned for still works. On these pages the tab boxes carry the parameter names, not the channel names. A plugin's name rarely fits one row — PitchBend Range and PitchBend Step would both read as PitchBen — so the tab box holds the first line and the row under it holds the second. Sixteen characters, and neighbours stop looking identical. The names are the plugin's own, so a port whose LV2 symbol is output reads Gain . Every other page keeps the channel tabs, which is where a dashed tab still says a channel is not sounding. Try it Select Group G (LEAD) and press CONTROL . That is page 1 — PRESET, CUTOFF, RESO, ENV, DECAY, LEVEL, REVERB, DELAY. Press the right arrow beside the display. Page 2. The names change to the plugin's own — abbreviated to fit, in the order the plugin lists them. Keep pressing. Each page is eight more ports. A large synth runs to several pages. Turn any of them. Each port is driven as a percentage of its own range, so a knob behaves the same whether the port runs 0–1 or 0–20000. Hold TEMPO and turn the same knob. Twice as fast. Hold it to get near, let go to land. Press CONTROL again to jump straight back to page 1 rather than paging around. How it works The four synth knobs follow the plugin that is loaded , not the one the snapshot shipped with. Change a chain's engine from the touchscreen and CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY rebind to the new plugin's own ports. Host plumbing is filtered out. Plugins publish ports no player can use — freewheel flags, latency reports, enable switches that are not really switches. Those are recognised and dropped, so a generated page is eight things you might actually turn. Discreteness is respected. A port with a handful of positions steps in whole units; a continuous one moves by percentage with the remainder carried, so slow turns still move it. A port with named positions steps between those names and never lands between two of them. TEMPO changes how far a turn goes, never what it sets. A speed, not a mode: nothing latches, and the same knob reaches the same values either way. It applies to every encoder on the instrument, not only these. Switches: the eight buttons above the knobs A plugin does not publish one kind of control, it publishes three. Continuous ones are knobs — cutoff, resonance. Switches are not: a filter type is LP24 or BP , an oscillator is saw or square , a section is on or off. Turning a knob between two words is the wrong gesture for it, and it used to show you a number where the plugin had a name. In CONTROL, F1–F8 are that page's switches — each button directly above the knob that owns the same column. Press it and the switch advances to its next position, wrapping round at the end. The column shows the plugin's own word, and the bar under it fills left to right to say where in the list you are — empty or full on a two-position switch. The knob still works. It walks the same positions one at a time and stops at each end instead of wrapping. Use the button to cycle, the knob to arrive. Try it Select a synth channel — F, G or H — and press CONTROL . Page right until a column shows a word rather than a four-digit number. Press the F button above that column , and keep pressing. The word changes and comes back round to where it started; the button lights whenever the switch is off its first position. Turn the knob below it. Same positions, one per detent, stopping at each end. What this costs, and where mute went F1–F8 are the mutes everywhere else, and in CONTROL they are not. Hold SHIFT and they mute again , in CONTROL only; SOLO + F still solos there as it does in every other mode. No other mode is touched. A dark F button in CONTROL means that column carries no switch — and the button does nothing, rather than doing something you did not ask for. On a drum channel, and on CONTROL page 1, that is the whole row. While MOD is held or latched the row is dark and inert. MOD already makes the pads inert and turns every knob into a modulation depth, and that gesture is supposed to change nothing. What it refuses, and why A one-shot trigger is not offered as a switch. Some plugins publish a port with a single named position — a panic or a re-init. Firing one off a button that used to be a mute is not a thing to discover by accident, so those are left alone. A role the plugin has no port for draws dead. If a loaded synth publishes no resonance, the RESO column greys out and its encoder does nothing at all. That is the same law the whole surface follows: a knob with no source is drawn dead rather than showing a number it cannot move. A knob that silently does nothing is the worst object on a control surface, because you cannot tell it apart from a broken one. See also Sound and presets — page 1, and changing the engine underneath it Modulation — every generated port can carry a modulator

title: Generating patterns

headings.text: RATCHET — a step that fires more than once
The CHANCE ramp — the kit thins out and re-forms
HALF and DOUBLE — the same rhythm, at another speed
The ratchet ramp — the roll into the drop
Reroll — two buttons that ask for a different bar

body: Generating patterns You do not draw a beat. You set hits, rotation and randomness, and the generator writes the notes. This is the machine's centre — everything else colours what happens here. What it is The driver writes real notes into Zynthian's own sequencer . Not a private buffer: because they are real notes in the real sequencer, patterns persist in snapshots and the touchscreen pattern editor mirrors exactly what the pads show. There are two generators, and every channel runs one of them: Euclidean , on the five drum channels. Given a step count and a hit count, hits spread as evenly as the grid allows, then rotate. Two Turing machines , on each of the three voices. One shift register is read as pitch, the other as which steps sound. Each is clocked once per pass and mutated by its own knob — MELODY and RHYTHM — so a melody can evolve over a rhythm that stays exactly where you put it. Which generator a channel runs is not fixed to its engine — see Sound and presets . Try it The drums. Press Play , then Group A to select KICK, then STEP . Turn encoder 1 (HITS) to 4. That is four-on-the-floor. Turn encoder 2 (ROTATE). The same four hits slide around the bar without changing how many there are. Turn HITS to 5. Five in sixteen is the clave. Try 3 in 8 for tresillo, or 7 in 16 for the busy one that still swings. The voices. Press Group F for BASS, still in STEP. Turn encoder 3 (MELODY) to about 30. The bassline starts fishing: every pass mutates one bit, so the line keeps turning into a neighbouring line. When a phrase goes past that you want, snap MELODY back to 0. The cell reads LOCK and that line is frozen, bit for bit, until you move the knob again. Missed it? Press NOTE REPEAT . It gives the previous line back and sets both knobs to 0 so it holds. Now put MELODY at LOCK and turn encoder 4 (RHYTHM) to about 30. The opposite: the notes hold still while steps appear and disappear underneath them. Both at LOCK, then tap pads in STEP mode. Each tap turns a step on or off, and it stays — tap step 1 and step 9, then turn MELODY up, and you have two notes evolving on the beat you chose. A KICK B SNAR C CLAP D CHAT HITS 0004 ROTATE 0000 DIVIDE 1/16 LENGTH 0016 The drum STEP page. HITS and ROTATE are the two you play with; DIVIDE and LENGTH set the frame. How it works The drum STEP page is HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE, LENGTH, VELO, CHANCE, SWING. HITS and ROTATE are the two you play with; the rest set the frame. CHANCE is how often a hit actually fires — drop it and the pattern starts breathing rather than repeating. The voice STEP page is DIVIDE, GATE, MELODY, RHYTHM, LENGTH, OCTAVE, RANGE, VELO. The two generators sit side by side because they are one idea. LENGTH here is the pitch register’s length in bits, not a bar count. GATE is how long each note holds — up to eight steps, so a pad can be a drone. The pitch value is quantised to ROOT and SCALE from the ALL page, then placed by OCTAVE and RANGE. MELODY is the instrument’s main gesture. Set it to 20–40 and the voice fishes. Snap it to 0 the moment you hear something worth keeping. The cell reads LOCK rather than a number, deliberately: a number could be a coincidence, while LOCK means nothing will rewrite that pattern at all. Both ends of MELODY are periodic, and only the middle is unpredictable. This surprises everyone once, so it is worth knowing before it happens to you: MELODY What you get LOCK (0) the same bar, bit for bit, forever 20–40 the line fishes — a neighbouring line each pass. This is the useful range around 50 the most unpredictable it gets 100 a two-bar loop. Not chaos At 100 every fed-back bit is flipped rather than sometimes flipped, so one pass gives you the exact inverse of the register and the next gives you the original back — pattern, inverse, pattern, inverse. It sounds like the generator has stopped evolving, and in a sense it has: it is evolving into a cycle of two. If you want it to keep surprising you, keep it below about 60. The same is true of RHYTHM, for the same reason. RHYTHM is the same gesture applied to the beat. Same range, same LOCK at zero, same freeze. Which steps sound is its own register, one bit per step, so it is independent of the notes: either can run while the other holds. A pad tap in STEP mode flips one of those bits, which is why a rhythm you tap in by hand survives everything — it is not an edit sitting on top of the generator, it is the generator. Structure lands on the bar; timbre lands instantly. A change to what the pattern is waits for the channel's own next wrap, so the groove never jumps under your hand. DIVIDE and LENGTH show in angle brackets — >1/8< — while a change is waiting to take. What it refuses, and why Pattern length is quantised to whole beats, and always will be. The sequencer stores a pattern as a number of beats, so the reachable step counts are whole beats times the steps in a beat. Turning LENGTH lands on the nearest count that exists rather than refusing to move — so if the number skips past where you aimed, that is the grid and not a fault. Which step counts you can reach depends on DIVIDE, not on the sequencer. At 1/16 a beat is four steps, so LENGTH moves in fours: 4, 8, 12, 16. At 1/4 a beat is one step, so every count from 1 to 16 is available. An odd number that DIVIDE cannot express is not missing from the instrument — it is on another division. A silent channel says so. HITS at 0 is a silent channel, not a broken one, and CHANCE at 0 emits nothing at all. Both draw the channel's tab dashed — the instrument's one mechanism for explaining silence. Read the tab row before suspecting the rig. Lengths that do not agree LENGTH is per channel, and nothing makes the eight agree. Give the kick four beats and the hat three, and they start together, drift apart, and meet again twelve beats later. Nothing is generating that — it is two loops of different lengths running side by side, which is the oldest trick in machine music and costs one encoder turn here. Set it on the STEP page with LENGTH . Every other channel is untouched, because length was never global. Which lengths each division reaches A pattern has to fit the sixteen pads, so the finer the division, the fewer beats it holds: DIVIDE Beats you can set Steps that gives 1/32 1–2 8, 16 1/16 1–4 4, 8, 12, 16 1/8 1–8 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 1/16T 1–2 6, 12 1/8T 1–5 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 1/4 1–16 every count from 1 to 16 Odd beat counts live at 1/8, 1/8T and 1/4. Three, five and seven beats are all reachable there. At 1/16 and finer they are not — a five-beat pattern at 1/16 would be twenty steps and there are sixteen pads to show it on. Try it Leave the kick on group A at four beats. Put a hat on group B, set DIVIDE to 1/8 and turn LENGTH down to three beats. Let it run: the hat walks around the kick and lands back on the one every twelve beats. Take group C to five beats and the three of them do not agree again for sixty. Shortening keeps the steps that fit and drops the ones past the new end; growing back leaves the new steps empty rather than restoring what a shrink discarded. A step that sounds sometimes Hold SHIFT and tap a step to set how often it plays. Each press steps it down — always, three times in four, half the time, one time in four — and the fifth press brings it back to always. A bare tap still turns the step on and off; SHIFT is what changes the odds. While SHIFT is held the pads show the odds instead of the pattern. Each step takes its own colour, brightest magenta for always, then red, then orange, and a cool pale blue for the rarest — so the one that hardly ever fires is obvious without comparing it to its neighbours. Let go and the step picture comes back. The white playhead keeps sweeping over the top either way. This is the gentlest way to make a bar stop repeating itself. A hat at three-quarters and a clap at half will not play the same bar twice, but the pattern you wrote is still the pattern — nothing is being regenerated behind your back. It is safe on a take you have recorded. Setting the odds does not rewrite the pattern: no step is moved, added or removed, so unlike turning HITS or ROTATE it cannot hand your take back to the generator. It costs nothing to try mid-jam, and the odds are saved in the snapshot with everything else. RATCHET — a step that fires more than once Encoder 8 on a drum's STEP page was empty. It is RATCHET now. Turn it up and every step of that channel fires two, three or four times inside its own slot — a roll rather than a hit. It reads OFF at the bottom, because one hit is not a ratchet. It applies to the whole channel, not one step, which is what makes it a knob rather than an edit: turn it up for a bar of rolls and back down again without touching the pattern you wrote. The CHANCE ramp — the kit thins out and re-forms New, and not yet played in. The CHANCE ramp went onto the rig with the phrase clock and ARM. What follows describes what the instrument does; it has not been through a session on the hardware yet. Hold ARM — that is SELECT — tap pad 2, then tap a length. The gesture is on The surface ; this is what it does. From the landing bar every channel's play chance walks down, one step per bar. Halfway through the length all eight are at one time in four — still playing, but most of it missing — and over the second half they walk back up. An eight-bar ramp is four bars falling apart and four bars coming back. It lands back on each channel's own value, not on always. A channel sitting at half the time comes back at half the time. Assuming everything wants to be at full is exactly how a channel saved quiet comes back loud, and this does not do it. A channel already at one time in four or below is left alone. A breakdown that made a quiet channel louder would be the gesture backwards. It is safe on a take you recorded. Play chance belongs to the pattern rather than to the notes: nothing is regenerated, no step is moved, added or removed, and the ramp writes once per bar rather than continuously. Same reason SHIFT + pad is safe. Play chance is in the snapshot, so a set saved mid-ramp saves the thinned values. Let it finish before you save. HALF and DOUBLE — the same rhythm, at another speed Arm HALF or DOUBLE and every generated channel changes speed on the bar, then changes back. The pattern is not redrawn coarser or finer: the step count is kept and the beat count moves with the division, so what you hear is the rhythm you already had, played at half or twice the speed. Some channels cannot make the move, and the display says how many did. HALF 5/8 means five of the eight went. A division needs somewhere to go: 1/8 triplet has no half-speed partner, 1/4 has none either, and 1/32 and 1/16 triplet cannot double. Double-time also needs an even number of beats to halve. A channel that cannot move is left exactly as it was rather than approximated. Straight stays straight and triplet stays triplet. A speed change that turned a straight channel into a triplet one would be a second, unasked-for change riding along with the first. It comes back to what was captured , not to a calculated opposite — drift, reroll and the encoders can all move a channel while the macro is out, and only the snapshot taken at the moment it fired is reliable. Channels you have recorded onto are left alone. The move regenerates from the generator settings, and a take has none to regenerate from. Under polymeter it can arrive up to a bar late on the odd channels. The macro fires on the phrase bar, but a structure change is taken at each channel’s own wrap — the same rule that stops a division change tripping the groove mid-bar. On a rig where every channel is four beats the question never comes up. The ratchet ramp — the roll into the drop Arm the ratchet ramp and every note subdivides further each bar , arriving at x4 exactly on the last bar of the length you chose. A four-bar arm walks 1–2–3–4; a two-bar arm goes 1 then 4. It always arrives — a build that stopped at x3 because you armed three bars would be a build that never lands. Each channel goes back to its own RATCHET setting afterwards, so a channel you had already left ratcheting comes back ratcheting. Recorded channels are skipped , for the same reason as above: the ramp rewrites the pattern from the generator settings each bar. Reroll — two buttons that ask for a different bar Hold PATTERN or SCENE to reroll the channel you are on. Hold, do not tap — let go early and nothing happens. A drum channel gets a new hit count and rotation; a channel played by the Turing register gets a new rhythm and a new play chance, and its MELODY is left at LOCK so you hear the new line held rather than already drifting. Hold SHIFT with them to reroll a whole family at once. SHIFT + PATTERN rerolls every sampler channel, SHIFT + SCENE every synth. That split follows the engine , not how the channel is being played — a drum sampler switched to Turing is still a sampler, so asking for new synth lines never hands you a new drum pattern as well. The two buttons light to show which family you are standing in. It lands on the bar, and the wait is the point. While it is pending the display reads REROLL> and the tabs of the channels it will hit are drawn dotted , so you see what is about to change before it does. Press the same button again before it lands and it is cancelled. It never touches a channel you have recorded on. Those channels are simply left out, and their tabs stay undotted — the drums have no undo, so a reroll that included them would be a data-loss button. If you want a recorded channel rerolled, hand it back first with ERASE + Group. It cannot leave a channel silent. A drum always keeps at least one hit, a voice always keeps some steps and a play chance above a floor. Silence with nothing to explain it is the one thing this instrument refuses to produce, and a reroll that muted a channel by accident would be exactly that. ERASE and the same button puts it back — one deep. ERASE is the take-it-back gesture everywhere on this instrument, and SHIFT is spoken for here. See also Modulation — how to make these values move on their own, and why the generator's own knobs refuse it Playing and recording — playing over the generator, and taking a pattern from it The surface — reading the tabs, and what to check when it goes quiet

title: Mixing and effects

headings.text: DROP — everything falls away but the ones you kept
BREAK — fall out now, come back on the bar
The master insert — one filter across the whole mix
The effects this is proven on
Five that are out, and why

body: Mixing and effects Balancing eight channels from eight knobs, the two effects every channel feeds, and the handful of settings that belong to the machine rather than to a channel. What it is Every channel carries its own reverb and delay send on encoders 7 and 8, feeding two shared effects. Sixteen insert hosts in total — a TAP Stereo Echo and a TAP Reverberator on every one of the eight channels. The sends are post-fader , so pulling a channel down takes its tail with it rather than leaving a ghost of it hanging in the reverb. Try it Press VOLUME. That is MIXER mode: one control across all eight channels at once, rather than eight controls on one channel. Turn any encoder. Each one is a channel's LEVEL. This is the page for balancing. Press the right arrow beside the display. The ring steps to REVERB, then DELAY — the same eight channels, a different send. Press VOLUME again to jump back to page 1 rather than paging round. Press AUTO. That is FILTER: CUTOFF and RESO across the row. Notice the five drum columns are drawn dead — see below. Press ALL. Now the eight encoders are the machine's globals: ROOT, SCALE, BPM, MASTER, REVSIZE, REVTYPE, DLYTIME, DLYFBK. How it works A spread page is one verb across eight channels. MIXER and FILTER are both spreads; CONTROL and STEP are the other shape, eight verbs on one channel. That is the whole grammar of the surface, and every page is one or the other. ROOT and SCALE wait for the bar , like everything else that changes what the pattern is. The rest of the globals land instantly. Group button brightness tracks each channel's level , so the row shows the balance without reading anything — and the peak meters on the display run live. DROP — everything falls away but the ones you kept New, and not yet played in. DROP went onto the rig with the phrase clock and ARM. What follows describes what the instrument does; it has not been through a session on the hardware yet. Hold ARM — that is SELECT — tap pad 1, then tap a length. The gesture itself is on The surface ; this is what lands. The Group buttons nominate the survivors while ARM is held. Tap A–H to add or drop a channel from the list, and the Group row stops reporting the mix and reports the nomination instead: full for a survivor, dim for everything else. While the modifier is down that row answers one question and no other. The list sticks between holds, so a kick-and-bass drop stays armed the way you left it. Nominate nothing and the drop takes all eight, which is a real setting rather than an unfinished one. On the landing bar every channel you did not nominate is muted. It is the mixer strip, not the sequencer — the same mute F1–F8 set — so it takes each channel's reverb and delay tail with it, and the tabs of the silenced channels draw dashed for as long as it runs. A silent channel still says why, even in the middle of a performance. The length is both numbers. Arm a drop over four bars and it fires four bars from now and lasts four bars. There is no second gesture for the duration. What comes back is exactly what was there. The mute picture is captured the instant the drop fires and restored unchanged — never "everything on". A channel you had muted by hand before the drop is still muted after it. Cancelling during a drop leaves the mutes where they are. The return is itself pending, and a bare ARM tap cancels everything pending — so cancel mid-drop and the room stays quiet. Lift the mutes with F1–F8. BREAK — fall out now, come back on the bar BREAK is DROP with its two ends swapped. Arm it and the channels you did not nominate fall silent immediately; they come back on the bar the length names. It is the breakdown you fall into rather than build to, with the drums returning exactly on the one, counted for you. Everything else is DROP’s: the same survivors on the Group buttons, the same snapshot of who was already muted, the same restore. The length means only when it ends — there is no waiting for it to start. Only one of DROP and BREAK can be armed at a time. They share one snapshot of the mutes, so arming either drops the other. The master insert — one filter across the whole mix The Main chain carries a filter, and ALL → MAIN reaches it. It sits between the mixer and the card, so it hears everything: all eight channels, their reverb and delay, the drop, the ramp, everything. It loads wide open and inaudible . That is deliberate rather than incidental — at the plugin’s own factory settings the cutoff sits below the point where it stops passing audio at all, so the snapshot writes every one of its controls explicitly instead of trusting a default. If the instrument ever goes completely silent with every channel looking healthy, look here first and open the cutoff. It is the one control on the rig that can silence all eight channels at once, and below roughly a third of its range it is genuinely silent rather than just dark. One instance, not eight — which is why it is affordable at all. The per-channel reverb and delay sit on every chain, so an effect there costs eight times what it looks like. The effects this is proven on The same insert pair sits on all eight chains, so an effect costs eight times what it looks like. That is where this Pi runs out of headroom — not on the synths. Every plugin below is in a shipped snapshot and has been measured running. Plugin What it is TAP Reverberator algorithmic reverb, and the factory one — it has a real wet level, which is rarer than it sounds TAP Stereo Echo stereo delay, the factory partner, also a true wet send Dragonfly Hall Reverb large algorithmic hall Dragonfly Room Reverb small-room algorithmic reverb Dragonfly Early Reflections reflections only, no tail — space without wash Tal-Reverb-II / Tal-Reverb-III plate-flavoured algorithmic reverbs Shiroverb diffuse ambient reverb Roomy compact room reverb Tal-Dub-3 dub delay — filtered repeats that degrade the way tape does Regrader degrading delay: each repeat loses bits and sample rate Modulay modulated delay, chorused repeats GxEcho-Stereo stereo echo Gxdigital_delay_st clean digital stereo delay YK Chorus chorus Multivoice Chorus multi-voice chorus, thicker and slower Calf Vinyl vinyl noise, crackle and wear Calf Tape Simulator tape wow, flutter and saturation MDA RingMod ring modulator TAP AutoPanner auto-panner Ping Pong Pan ping-pong panner ZamEQ2 · 3 Band EQ parametric and three-band EQ ZamCompX2 stereo compressor What eight instances actually cost Measured on the rig at 512 frames and 48 kHz, with eight synths playing and only the insert pair changed: Insert pair Mean CPU Xruns TAP Stereo Echo + TAP Reverberator 18.5 % 0 Calf Vinyl + Tal-Reverb-III 25.4 % 0 Roomy + Tal-Reverb-II 25.8 % 0 Shiroverb + Tal-Reverb-III 28.1 % 0 Modulay + Dragonfly Hall Reverb 29.8 % 0 YK Chorus + Dragonfly Room Reverb 36.5 % 0 Five that are out, and why Plugin Measured at eight instances Aether 61.6 % with real xruns — still 49 % in the lighter three-synth layout CHOWTapeModel 82.4 % and 62 xruns ChowPhaserStereo 91.6 % — eleven of twenty-four plugin hosts never start at all Roboverb 93.8 % and 406 xruns Two Dragonfly reverbs together 52.7 %; either one alone is about 30 % Each was proven guilty by elimination — its partner in the pair measured clean elsewhere — and each was replaced in the presets that carried it. Loading without an error is not running without a glitch , which is the whole reason these numbers exist. Watch what a plugin calls a wet control. Several well-known reverbs turn out to crossfade dry against wet rather than offering a send, so turning the mix up takes the dry signal away with it. The factory pair was chosen by measuring that with an impulse, one plugin at a time. If you swap in your own, check it the same way before trusting the REVERB and DELAY encoders. What it refuses, and why FILTER's five drum columns draw dead. Only the three voices answer it. The drum channels run a sampler, and there is no filter in that chain to reach — so rather than offering a knob that would do nothing, the columns grey out. There is no drum filter in this version. That is worth saying plainly so you do not go hunting for one: filtering drums needs a filter plugin per channel, which costs eight more plugin hosts, and it has not been built. title: Modulation

headings.text: Drift — when the pattern itself moves
RISE — a sweep that happens once
The big encoder — how much everything moves

body: Modulation Set how a value moves instead of what it is. Quick start gets you playing; this page is the second dimension underneath every knob you already know. What it is MOD is the SWING button. Hold it and every encoder stops setting a value and starts setting how that value moves . Tap it instead and it latches, so both hands are free. The button says which one you did: steady while you hold it, blinking while it is latched. Same blink GRID uses for an overridden kind, so the panel has one vocabulary and not two. It matters because a latched MOD outlives your finger — the encoders keep meaning depth and the refused columns keep their bars off until you tap it again. It is not a mode. It adds no page, no ring entry, and nothing to memorise: the map of parameters you already know does not change, and MOD gives every one of them a second dimension in the same place. It costs no plugin instances, and nothing is created or destroyed while you play. Try it Press Play and select a voice — Group G is LEAD. Press CONTROL. Encoder 2 is CUTOFF. Hold SWING — that is MOD — and turn encoder 2. The column's name gains a ~ and its bar grows a dashed span. You are setting how far the cutoff will travel, not where it sits. A small turn gives a narrow sweep; a bigger turn a broader one. Let go of SWING and listen. The filter sweeps on its own. Keep MOD held and tap pad 1 , then pad 12 . Pads 1–12 are the rates, slowest first: sixteen bars per cycle at one end, a sixteenth at the other. You should hear the sweep speed up dramatically between the two. Tap pads 13–16 for the four shapes — triangle, ramp, square, and sample-and-hold, which jumps to a new value each cycle and holds it there. Release MOD and turn encoder 2 again. Now you are steering the base — the centre the sweep moves around — and the sweep follows you there. Hold SWING and ERASE together and turn encoder 2. The modulation stops and the value returns to where you set it, not to wherever the sweep happened to stop. E OHAT F BASS G LEAD H PADS PRESET BA01 CUTOFF~ 0064 RESO 0032 ENV 0048 CUTOFF carries a modulator: the name gains a ~ , the bar shows the range it sweeps, and the value cell still reads the base — the number your hand owns. How it works Depth is bipolar, and centre is off. Turning back to the middle does not leave a dormant modulator behind — it removes it. The fastest way to stop something moving is to put its depth back where it started. Rates are locked to the bar , so a modulator lines up with the pattern it is colouring rather than drifting against it. Twelve rates and four shapes fill the sixteen pads exactly, with nothing unreachable. The value cell always shows the base. Motion lives on the indicator bar: a dashed span across the range the modulator covers, and a small tick travelling inside it. A fast modulator blurs into a static span, and that is honest — the span is the truth, the tick is a courtesy. On 1-bit glass refreshing five times a second, animating the number would just make it unreadable. On a spread page it is eight at once. Press VOLUME for the mixer, then MOD and each encoder in turn, and every channel gets its own modulator on the same control. They do not run in lockstep: each starts its cycle at the moment you bind it, so binding them one after another spreads them around the bar and the row breathes rather than pumps. It is saved. Modulators go into the snapshot with their depth, rate, shape and position, and the value stored is the base you set rather than wherever the sweep happened to be. Load the set tomorrow and they are still running, still spread apart. What it refuses, and why MOD will not bind to anything that rewrites the pattern. While MOD is down, those columns lose their bar — the name and the value stay, because they are still live controls; they just cannot be modulated. So the rule under MOD is simple: a bar means you can bind here . HITS · ROTATE · MELODY · RHYTHM · CHANCE · VELO · GATE · DIVIDE · LENGTH · KIT · PRESET · ROOT · SCALE The refusal is the design, not a gap. A modulator writes several times a second. A knob that rewrites the pattern would tear the line up continuously — and on a channel you had recorded onto, it would destroy your take with nothing on the surface explaining why. Nothing MOD can do will touch a recorded take. Generation moving on its own is a genuinely good idea and it is coming, but it needs its own answer to that question first. Drift — when the pattern itself moves Everything above modulates the sound. Drift modulates the pattern. Bind it to HITS and the channel gains and loses hits on its own; bind it to ROTATE and the bar turns under itself; bind it to CHANCE and the whole channel thins out and comes back. The arrangement evolves instead of the tone. You bind it exactly like any other modulator — hold MOD and turn HITS, ROTATE or CHANCE on the STEP page. MOD + pad sets its rate and shape as usual, and the pad legend shows them. It moves once per bar, not continuously. A pattern cannot be redrawn five times a second without tearing the groove apart, so drift waits for the pattern to come round and changes it there. At the slowest rate a full breath in and out takes about half a minute; the fastest rates change something every bar. Drift refuses to touch a channel you have recorded on, and says so. Its columns lose their bars there, exactly like any other refusal. This is the one rule that makes drift safe to leave running: a pattern rewritten with nobody touching the panel would otherwise erase your take while you played. If you record onto a channel that is already drifting, the drift stops. It is checked every bar, not only when you bind it, so your take is safe the moment it exists. The drift is not thrown away — hand the channel back with ERASE + Group and it picks up where it left off. The pads become the menu While MOD is down the sixteen pads stop showing your pattern and show the modulation menu instead. They were always the menu — a pad hit under MOD has always set a rate or a shape — they just used to keep drawing steps while they did it. Now they say what they are. The top three rows are the twelve rates , slower on the left, faster to the right and down. The bottom row is the four shapes — triangle, ramp, square, and sample-and-hold. The pads used to fade, each at its own rate and in its own shape, so you could see what a setting felt like before choosing it. That is gone, for the same reason the tick is — repainting sixteen pads on a timer floods the connection the buttons come back on. The grid is still now, and the rate you have chosen is named on the label. The rate and shape you are using are lit full , brighter than the rest, so what is selected reads at a glance. If every pad is dim and still, nothing is bound yet. MOD + pad only has something to act on once a modulator exists, so rather than dance under a gesture that would do nothing, the pads say so. Bind one — MOD and turn any encoder with a bar — and the menu comes alive. There is no playhead here: under MOD the pads are not steps, so a sweep would point at nothing. Let MOD go and your pattern comes straight back. The rates span more than two hundred to one — the slowest is over half a minute per cycle, the fastest a tenth of a second. Further right and further down is faster; the label tells you exactly which one you are on. RISE — a sweep that happens once New, and not yet played in. RISE went onto the rig with the phrase clock and ARM. What follows describes what the instrument does; it has not been through a session on the hardware yet. A modulator normally cycles for ever. Hold ARM — that is SELECT — and tap a shape pad, and it sweeps once and stays where it ends. That is the riser: the cutoff climbs over eight bars and sits at the top instead of falling back down. It acts on the modulator you bound most recently , which is the same one MOD + pad has always steered. MOD latches, so there is no chord to catch: tap MOD, then hold ARM and tap pads 13–16. SHIFT still outranks both — a pad under SHIFT is a step's odds, whatever else is latched. Where it holds depends on the shape you tap , because holding at the end of one sweep is not the same place for all four: Pad Shape Once, it 13 triangle rises, falls, and holds at the bottom 14 ramp climbs all the way and holds at the top — this is the riser 15 square jumps to the top for the first half, drops, and holds at the bottom 16 sample-and-hold picks one value and holds it for the whole sweep Under a one-shot the rate pads mean length. Pads 1–12 are the same twelve numbers, sixteen bars down to a sixteenth, read as how long the whole sweep takes rather than how long one cycle takes. Tapping one restarts the sweep from that moment at the new length — which is also how you fire the same riser again. The sweep starts when you tap, not on the next downbeat. It runs for the length you chose from that instant and then holds, so aim the tap, or arm a long one and let it arrive. Nothing on the panel marks a modulator as one-shot. The column keeps its ~ and its dashed span and the pads keep their menu. You hear it rather than see it: the sweep arrives and stays there instead of coming back. It refuses exactly what MOD refuses. Running once is a shape, not a new permission: the pattern-rewriting columns still have no bar, and drift still refuses a channel you have recorded on. A one-shot is not saved as one. Reload the set and that modulator is cycling again — hold ARM and tap its shape pad to make it one-shot once more. To turn one back into a cycle without reloading, clear it with MOD + ERASE and that encoder, then bind it again. Clearing everything at once Hold MOD and ERASE and press ALL . Every modulator goes, and every value lands back where you put it. The markers vanish the instant you press it; the values themselves settle a moment later. That gap is deliberate — the instrument will not write twenty parameters inside a single button press, because doing that on the button thread once froze the whole machine. The big encoder — how much everything moves While MOD is latched, the big encoder scales every live modulator at once , from nothing up to about twice their set depth. One hand takes a static rig to a churning one and back. Every modulated column’s dashed span widens and narrows together as you turn, which is the most literal picture of what is happening. Turn it down to zero and everything parks; turn it back and every modulator returns to exactly the depth you gave it — the multiplier is kept separately rather than multiplied into the depths, so nothing is stranded at zero with no way back. This is the one exception to the big encoder being the page ring. While MOD is latched it is the depth knob instead. MOD’s own label on the page indicator is what tells you which of the two you are holding. Sweeps start with the phrase Every modulator counts from the phrase, not from when the instrument was switched on. An eight-bar sweep is the eight bars rather than an eight-bar sweep at some arbitrary offset, and starting the transport or pressing RESTART re-zeros the whole modulation system along with the bar count. The relative spread between modulators is kept, so eight LFOs that were chasing each other go on chasing each other.
