title: Playing and recording

headings.text: Capturing the jam to a file

body: Playing and recording The pads are the instrument. Hold REC while you play them and what you played is captured into the same pattern the generator writes — and from that moment the pattern is yours, not the machine's. What it is In CONTROL, ALL, MIXER and FILTER the sixteen pads play the selected channel. On a voice they are notes. On a drum every pad triggers that channel's own sound, because a drum channel is one sound — hearing CLAP while playing KICK would be the silent-channel confusion in a new costume. In STEP the pads are the step editor instead. A tap toggles that step, and the velocity of the tap becomes the step's velocity, so accents are played in rather than dialled. Step 0 is the top-left pad; the grid reads left to right, top to bottom. Try it Press Play , select Group F (BASS) and press CONTROL . Play the pads — that is the instrument. Hold REC and play a short phrase. Keep holding REC. Let go of the last pad while REC is still held , then release REC. Your phrase is in the pattern. Press STEP and look at the pads. The steps you played light amber ; the generated notes are still there underneath, dim or bright. Look at the page indicator. It reads PLAY — you own this pattern now, and the generator has stopped rewriting it. To give it back: hold ERASE and press Group F . Your take is gone and the generator resumes. That is deliberate and it is destructive. How it works Capture happens on release, not on press. A note's length is how long you held the pad, and that is not known until you let go. This has a consequence worth committing to memory: you must still be holding REC when you release the pad. Let go of REC first and the note sounds but is never captured. That is the same rule that lets you release REC without cutting off notes still ringing, so it is a trade rather than an oversight. Strikes quantise to the nearest step , wrapping at the end of the bar — nearest rather than next, so a strike landing a hair early is not pushed a step late. A note's length is clamped to what is left of the pattern. Recording adds; it does not overwrite. The generated line freezes where it is and your note goes on top, so a recorded step can hold two notes. An amber pad means your note is there and the generated one still is. A step that sounds but stays dark would be the defect. The page indicator reads REC while you are capturing , and REC-STOP if the transport is stopped — nothing is being captured then, and the surface says so rather than letting you play into nothing. Who owns the pattern The first captured note makes you the owner of that channel's pattern, and the generator stops rewriting it. The indicator reads PLAY for as long as that holds — including after a snapshot reload , because ownership is saved. Handing the pattern back is deliberate and destructive: your take is gone the moment it happens. There are two routes, and knowing which knobs do it is the difference between keeping a take and losing one. Route On a drum On a voice Gesture ERASE + the channel's Group button Knobs that hand back HITS, ROTATE, DIVIDE LENGTH, DIVIDE, MELODY, RHYTHM Knobs that keep the take LENGTH, VELO, CHANCE, SWING GATE, OCTAVE, RANGE, VELO Two details worth carrying: a drum's LENGTH keeps the take, because shortening a pattern preserves the steps that still fit; and MELODY and RHYTHM only hand back when they move off LOCK , since a locked generator rewrites nothing and could not undo your recording anyway. A knob has to actually move — brushing one does nothing. On a drum channel the amber colouring does not survive a snapshot reload, and that is not a lost take. A played drum note carries the same pitch as a generated one, so once the pattern is read back there is nothing left to tell the two apart. The notes are all there and the channel is still yours: the indicator still reads PLAY , and after a reload that indicator, not the pad colour, is the authority. On a voice the amber survives, because the played pitch is its own. Capturing the jam to a file SHIFT + REC starts and stops an audio recording. It captures the master — all eight channels, the effects, and anything a macro does to them — to a WAV on the Pi, alongside the other captures. It cannot collide with overdub, which is bare REC held . That is also why it is a chord rather than a long press: a long press of REC already is the overdub hold. REC’s light tells you which one you are in. Dim when a take is possible, full while you hold it for an overdub, and red while a recording is being written — including when you have moved to a page where overdub is not possible, so a running capture can never be invisible. What it refuses, and why You cannot record in STEP mode — there the pads belong to the step editor — and you cannot record while MOD is active , where they pick a modulator's rate and shape. In both cases the REC button is unlit . A lit REC would be promising a take it cannot make, so it goes dark rather than letting you play a phrase into nothing and wonder why it vanished. title: Saving your work

headings.text: What it will not carry, and why

body: Saving your work A snapshot holds the whole instrument — patterns, sounds, levels, and the driver's own state. Two things it cannot hold, and one trap in the web interface. Try it On the touchscreen (or through VNC in a browser), open the snapshot list and enter a bank. The first entry is Save as new snapshot . That is the one. To load, pick any snapshot in the list. Everything comes back — including which channels you had switched, and who owned each pattern. The trap In webconf's Snapshots page, the Name field and its checkmark RENAME THE SELECTED BANK. They do not save a snapshot. It looks exactly like a save box. It is not one. Save from the touchscreen or VNC. What a snapshot carries The patterns themselves, play chance and swing, mixer levels and mutes, both effect sends per channel, and each channel's kit or preset. Plus the driver's own state, which exists nowhere else: every voice's Turing register and its four-deep undo ring, the voice parameters, the globals, which channels you switched kind on , who owns each pattern , your modulators — depth, rate, shape, position and base — and the mode and page you were in. A set saved mid-sweep comes back at the value you dialled in, not wherever a modulator happened to be when you saved. What it will not carry, and why A mute set on the sequencer does not persist. Mute the mixer strip instead — that is in the snapshot, and it shows on the touchscreen mixer too. The phrase count and anything armed are not saved. The bar count is a live ruler rather than a position — it starts again from one on the next Play — and a macro still counting down is gone with it. A one-shot modulator comes back cycling, and a set saved while a drop is running saves those mutes, because mixer mutes are exactly what a snapshot does carry. Amber provenance on a drum channel does not survive a reload. Your take does; the colour does not. A played drum note has the same pitch as a generated one, so once the pattern is read back nothing can tell them apart. The PLAY indicator remains the authority. See also Playing and recording — what ownership means, and why amber matters Modulation — modulators are saved running

title: Sound and presets

headings.text: The synth engines this is proven on

body: Sound and presets What each channel sounds like, how to change it while the rig plays, and how to make a channel behave as something its engine is not. What it is CONTROL is the sound page, and it follows the engine. A drum engine gives you KIT and SAMPLE; a synth engine gives you PRESET, CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY. Encoders 6, 7 and 8 are LEVEL, REVERB and DELAY on every channel — the same three controls in the same place, always. The engine decides, not the behaviour. A sampler played by the Turing register still has a kit and a sample, so it still shows them. Switching a channel's kind changes how it is played, never what it is. Every channel keeps its engine for the life of the snapshot. Nothing is created or destroyed while you play, because building a plugin rebuilds the audio graph and that is a hole in the sound. Try it Select Group A (KICK) and press CONTROL . Encoder 1 is KIT, encoder 2 is SAMPLE. Turn SAMPLE. The kick changes to another sound inside the same kit, immediately. Press the button to the right of the big encoder. Same effect — it steps the selected channel's sound without using an encoder. Hold SHIFT and press it again. Now it steps the kit rather than the sample. Only a drum engine has kits, so on a synth channel this does nothing. Select Group G (LEAD) and press CONTROL . Now encoder 1 is PRESET and encoders 2–5 are CUTOFF, RESO, ENV and DECAY. Turn CUTOFF. You are driving the synth that is actually loaded, not a fixed idea of one. Now the interesting one. Select Group E (OHAT) and hold SHIFT while pressing GRID . The channel changes what it behaves as. Do it again to change back. One channel arrives switched E · OHAT ships as a voice. It keeps its Simmons kit and its sampler, but the Turing register drives it rather than euclid, so it walks between samples instead of laying down a straight hat. If your open hat wanders and you did not ask it to, that is the factory state and not a fault . Press SHIFT + GRID on E to hear it as an ordinary euclidean hat. It ships that way so the switch is audible the moment you plug in. How switching a kind works SHIFT + GRID switches the selected channel between drum and voice behaviour. The engine is never swapped. A drum kit gets the Turing generator, and a synth gets euclid. On a sampler the register walks the kit's own note list rather than ROOT and SCALE, because there a note selects a sample and scale-quantising would land most steps on empty keys — silence with nothing to explain it. On a synth, euclid becomes a root pulse : ROOT plus that channel's OCTAVE, on every hit. Each channel keeps a separate set of parameters per kind, so switching back and forth does not cost you your settings. Pattern length and division deliberately do not move: they are pattern time, not kind, and the groove must not jump under a switch. The surface says when a channel is not itself. The page indicator reads VOX or DRM , and GRID blinks for as long as the selected channel is on an overridden kind. Switching back clears the override rather than pinning the channel to a kind it merely happens to have today — so a later snapshot putting a different engine on that chain is not overruled by a stale choice nobody remembers making. What it refuses, and why A switch rewrites the pattern , so on a channel you have recorded onto it hands the pattern back to the generator and your take is gone. Hand-edited steps do not survive either, for the same reason turning HITS does not — switching rewrites the line from the generator. A voice switched to drum may arrive silent , because its HITS can read back as 0. The tab draws dashed to say so. That is not a defect: turn HITS up. A defect that was published here has been withdrawn. The buttons beside the big encoder were reported to step a preset once and then stick. They never did: they step every press. What stuck was the name . The value was drawn in a font that fits four characters, and preset banks are full of neighbours that agree on their first four — a padthv1 bank of 67 patches has six called Dusk , Dusk2 … Dusk6 , and stepping walks a bank alphabetically. Six presses, one word on the screen, six variants of one pad. Names now draw in the small font at nine characters and keep their trailing digits , so every press shows its move. Fifty starting points The rig ships with fifty more snapshots beside the factory one , numbered 031 to 080 in bank 000 . Ten each of house, deep house, minimal, dub and trance, from 118 to 140 BPM, across 21 synth engines and 24 drum machines. They are fixed arrangements, not generative patches. Every voice arrives at LOCK — MELODY and RHYTHM both 0 — and nothing is modulated. Load one and it plays the same bar until you change something. That is deliberate: the rest of this instrument is about evolution, and these are the places to start from. Turn MELODY up and the preset becomes generative under your hands. The five drum channels keep their roles. A is always the kick and E always the open hat; what changes is the machine — TR909 for house, TR808 and CR78 for dub, TR606 for minimal, SP-1200 for lo-fi. Kits are mixed across channels the way they are on a record, so a 909 kick can sit under an 808 clap. 031 – 060 use the delay and reverb you already know. 061 – 080 replace that pair with something else on every chain — tape and chorus, vinyl and room, phaser and hall — a different pair on each, none repeated. On those twenty, the REVERB and DELAY encoders still send to whatever now occupies those two slots, so the labels stay put while the sound does not. Load one from the touchscreen, inside bank 000 . Nothing is created or destroyed while you play, so a snapshot change is the one moment the audio graph is rebuilt. Twenty that never sit still Snapshots 081 – 100 are the opposite instrument. The fifty above hold still until you move something; these have almost no rhythm and twelve modulators each, all of them slow. A voice sounds once or twice a bar on an eight-step note, and everything else drifts. 081 – 090 are drones: all eight channels play as voices , each on its own synth. 091 – 100 are ambient — A to D stay drums, sparse and soft, and E to H are voices. Tempos run 52 to 90. These use SHIFT + GRID, saved. A channel plays as a voice only because the snapshot carries that override, so on a drone you will see GRID blinking and the page indicator reading VOX on channels that are normally drums. That is the instrument telling you the channel is not itself — it is the state, not a fault. Press SHIFT + GRID on one to hear it as a drum again. Four of the ambient presets leave E on its sampler rather than giving it a synth, so the Turing register walks the kit's own samples. It is the trick the factory snapshot uses on the same channel, and it sounds nothing like a synth pad. The modulation is bar-synced and deliberately slow — the slowest rate is a full sixteen bars, which at 60 BPM is a sweep over a minute long. Nothing here needs your hands to stay interesting. Turn any modulated knob and you steer the centre of its sweep rather than fighting it. The synth engines this is proven on Twenty-four LV2 synths, plus the sampler. Every one below is loaded by a shipped snapshot and has been run on the rig — eight instances at once in the drone presets, which is the hardest thing this instrument does. Nothing here is a recommendation from a plugin list; it is what has actually played. Engine What kind of synth it is Where it plays padthv1 additive pad synth — PADsynth, huge slow spectra factory, both packs Obxd virtual analogue poly, Oberheim OB-X voicing factory, both packs JC303 TB-303 emulation — mono acid bass, one filter, accent factory, both packs synthv1 four-oscillator subtractive poly both packs amsynth two-oscillator analogue-modelled subtractive both packs String machine divide-down string ensemble — one sound, done well both packs Monique monophonic virtual analogue, aggressive filters genre pack MDA JX10 two-oscillator virtual analogue poly both packs MDA DX10 FM poly — DX-flavoured, four voices of it both packs MDA ePiano modelled electric piano both packs Calf Monosynth subtractive mono, two filters in series or parallel both packs Calf Wavetable wavetable poly both packs MiMi-d virtual analogue poly both packs Triceratops three-oscillator virtual analogue poly with unison both packs Helm subtractive poly built around heavy modulation genre pack Odin2 semi-modular hybrid — analogue, wavetable and FM oscillators both packs Surge XT hybrid poly: wavetable, FM and subtractive in one voice both packs Noize Mak3r virtual analogue poly (TAL NoiseMaker) both packs Nekobi a second 303 — Nekobee, squarer than JC303 genre pack Mutated Instruments macro-oscillator voice: one control picks the synthesis model both packs Kars Karplus–Strong plucked string both packs RipplerX physically modelled resonators — strings, membranes, plates drone pack Vex three-oscillator subtractive poly with its own arpeggiator drone pack MiniOPL3 OPL3 chip emulation — two-operator FM, early-90s PC drone pack LinuxSampler the SFZ sampler behind every drum channel and the kit walk everywhere One synth is out. SO-kl5 Piano Synthesizer was in a drone preset and cost 57.6 % of a core with 11 xruns at eight instances; it was replaced with RipplerX and that preset now runs at 38.6 % with none. It is the only engine on this rig that failed — a probe carrying six otherwise-unproven synths at once measured 16.4 %, so synths are not what runs this Pi out of headroom. Effects are; see Mixing and effects . Any other LV2 synth Zynthian can load will work with the surface — the four page-1 knobs rebind by name and the generated pages are built from whatever it publishes. Untested means untested, not unsupported. RANGE narrows the kit walk When a drum channel is played by the Turing register, RANGE decides how much of the kit it may reach. It arrives at 1, which is one note : the channel keeps playing its own drum and the register decides only which steps sound . That is the useful thing most of the time — you get rhythm you could not have programmed, on the drum you chose. Turn it up and the walk widens outward from that drum , taking in its neighbours in the kit, until at 4 it may use the whole thing. That is where a hats channel starts hitting kicks, which is occasionally what you want and usually not. On a synth channel the same encoder still means octave spread; the column follows the engine, as the sound page always has. title: The surface

headings.text: The phrase — one bar count for the whole instrument
ARM — landing a change on a bar
PENDING — what is armed, and how to kill one
The mute grid — arrangement by pad
Beat repeat — squeeze it to one beat

body: The surface What every button does, how to read the two displays, and the list to work down when a channel goes quiet. Modes and pages Five buttons latch a mode, and exactly one is lit at any time. Button on the panel Mode The eight encoders become CONTROL CONTROL what the selected channel sounds like STEP STEP what the selected channel plays ALL ALL the machine's globals VOLUME MIXER one level across all eight channels AUTO FILTER one filter control across all eight channels A mode can carry more than one page. The arrows beside the display step through that mode's ring and wrap; the page name sits in the middle of the display. Each mode remembers its own page separately for drum and voice channels, so changing channel does not throw you onto a page you were not on. The big encoder does the same thing, and it is the faster way. Turn it and you walk the pages of whatever mode you are in — one page per click, either direction, no modifier and no press. It does this everywhere and it does nothing else, so it is the one control you never have to think about: whatever you are looking at, turning it shows you the next of it. Spin it quickly and it moves several pages rather than losing the ones it passed. Pressing the mode you are already in returns you to page 1 of that mode. It does not switch you anywhere — every mode button means the same thing twice over: this mode, from the top . Group A–H selects the channel. Pads, tabs and all eight encoders follow immediately, and the inverted tab on the display — never a Group LED — is the authority on which channel is selected. Reading the displays Both displays carry a tab row across the top — A–D on the left, E–H on the right — with four encoder columns under each. On a generated CONTROL page the tab row carries parameter names instead — that page is one channel's own plugin, and the names need the room. See Deep parameter control . Everywhere else the tab row is the channels: The inverted tab is the selected channel. A dashed tab means that channel is not sounding , whether it is muted at the mixer or silenced by its own generator. It is the one mechanism this instrument has for explaining silence, so read the tab row before assuming a fault. A KICK B SNAR C CLAP D CHAT KIT SP12 SAMPLE 0003 cutoff ---- reso ---- A drum channel on CONTROL. CUTOFF and RESO draw dead in lower case with ---- : a sampler has no filter to reach, and the encoder does nothing rather than pretending. The phrase — one bar count for the whole instrument New, and not yet played in. The phrase clock, ARM, DROP, the CHANCE ramp and RISE went onto the rig together. What follows describes what the instrument does; none of it has been through a session on the hardware yet. The page name on the display carries a bar number — STEP 5/16 — counting one to sixteen and starting again. It is one count for all eight channels, not one per channel. Each channel owns its own length, so eight channels can be on eight different bars; a count taken from any one of them would be a lie on the other seven. This one comes from the transport instead, so it stays true however far apart the lengths are — see lengths that do not agree . Bar 1 is the moment you press Play, and Restart re-zeros it along with the playheads — count and patterns are pulled back onto the one together. Stop and the number goes away rather than freezing, because a stuck number reads as a clock that has died. It is a live ruler, not a position: it is not saved, and it starts again from one on the next Play. Hold NAVIGATE and the sixteen pads become the phrase , one pad per bar: the bars behind you dim, the bar you are in full, the bars ahead dark. With the transport stopped every pad is dark. Let go and your pattern comes straight back. NAVIGATE changes what the pads show, not what they do. A pad hit while you hold it still toggles a step or plays the channel, exactly as it would without it. Read the phrase page, do not play it. The count is read thirty times a second, so anything scheduled against it lands within a few hundredths of a bar. That is close enough for a mute or a level, and deliberately not close enough for anything that has to sit on a step. ARM — landing a change on a bar SELECT is ARM. Hold it — it never latches — and compose two things on the pads: what is going to happen, and how many bars away . Pads while ARM is held What they are 1–6 the macro — DROP , CHANCE ramp , HALF , DOUBLE , BREAK , ratchet ramp . Amber, and the one you picked lights full 7 and 8 dark, and they do nothing. This is where later macros go 9–16 the length in bars — 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16. Green Pick the macro first, then the length. The length is the commit: tapping it arms the macro. A length on its own does nothing at all, because guessing which macro you meant would fire something you never named. The grid becomes a countdown the instant something is armed. One red pad per bar of the length you chose, going out from the top left as the bars pass, so the pads still lit are the bars still to come. While that is showing every pad is inert — reading the countdown must not also change it. Let ARM go without touching a pad and everything pending is cancelled. That is the same window a reroll gives you, and it cancels all rather than one for the same reason: a half-cancelled gesture is harder to think about than none. SELECT is the indicator once your hand has left it. Dark when nothing is armed, one flash per bar while a macro counts down, and steady through the bar it lands on. The flash is driven by the bar count rather than by a timer, so it cannot drift away from the thing it is counting. Arming with the transport stopped keeps the length and waits. There is no bar to count from yet, so nothing can fire; press Play and the macro lands that many bars in. SELECT sits steady rather than flashing meanwhile, because nothing is counting down yet. Arming a macro that is already pending replaces it instead of stacking a second one, so two drops can never land on different bars and fight over the same restore. With MOD active, ARM belongs to the modulators instead. MOD latches, so MOD held or latched plus ARM is the gesture that makes a modulator sweep once — see RISE . Tap MOD off first if you want to arm a macro. SHIFT outranks both : a pad under SHIFT is a step's odds, whatever else is latched. BREAK is the exception to the length. Every other macro fires in N bars; BREAK fires immediately and comes back in N. There is no “in N bars” for a gesture whose whole point is that it happens now. DROP and BREAK cannot both be armed. They are the same mechanism with its ends swapped and they share one snapshot of who was muted, so arming either quietly drops the other. Only one thing may own the mutes at a time. Each macro is written up where it lands: DROP and BREAK , the CHANCE ramp , HALF and DOUBLE , and the ratchet ramp . PENDING — what is armed, and how to kill one Go to ALL and turn the big encoder. The ALL ring has a second page now: one column per armed macro, soonest first, with the bars remaining and a bar counting down. With nothing armed it says NONE rather than drawing eight blank columns. Hold ERASE and turn the encoder under a column to cancel that one. Letting ARM go still cancels everything — that is the panic gesture and stays a single press. This is the surgical version. The columns are sorted by how soon each lands and only move when something really overtakes something else, so the page stays readable while it counts. FREEZE — stop the machine evolving PAD MODE is FREEZE, and it has two depths. Gesture What holds still Tap — latches MELODY, RHYTHM, drift and reroll. The notes stop changing under you — and the LFOs keep sweeping , so the sound goes on breathing Hold — momentary all of that plus the LFOs. Everything parks until you let go That is the surface’s standing rule — a tap latches, a hold is momentary — so there is nothing new to learn. Tap again to thaw. A frozen instrument says so three times over , because one that did not would read as a broken one: PAD MODE lights, the page indicator gains FRZ (or FRZ! for the total hold), and the RANDOM and RHYTHM columns lose their bars in the same grey MOD already uses for “this control cannot act right now”. The values stay — they are what resumes. A pending reroll is held, not thrown away. Its tab stays dashed and it fires on the next wrap after you thaw. Do not hold SHIFT and press PAD MODE. That combination never reaches the instrument at all: the USB daemon eats it for a mode of its own, where the pads program its internal sequence. It is a pre-existing trapdoor rather than anything FREEZE added, and the way out is to press PAD MODE without SHIFT until the pads behave again. The mute grid — arrangement by pad Hold MUTE and the sixteen pads become your eight channels, twice. Pads while MUTE is held What they do Top two rows, 1–8 mute and unmute channel A–H now Bottom two rows, 9–16 queue the same change to that channel’s next wrap Each pad wears its channel’s own colour, because hue is identity everywhere on this surface. Full means audible, dark means muted. A pad in the bottom half shows the change, not the state : half-lit when something is queued for that channel and dark when nothing is. Drawing the state there would only repeat the row above. Tap a queued pad twice and the queue is cancelled rather than reversed — the second press of a gesture is its undo everywhere else here. Pressing the instant pad also clears anything queued for that channel, so one strip never has two answers waiting. It is the mixer strip that mutes, the same one the F row uses, so it is in your snapshot and shows on the touchscreen mixer. Beat repeat — squeeze it to one beat Hold the transport’s ▶ STEP button. Every generated channel collapses to its first beat and loops it; let go and the patterns come straight back. One beat is the floor — a pattern’s length is whole beats and always will be, so there is no half-bar repeat. Worth knowing that a beat is a different size per channel: at 1/4 it is a single step, at 1/32 it is eight. The same gesture is a repeated hit on a coarse channel and a tight stutter on a fine one. Channels you have recorded onto are skipped , and the page indicator says how many it took — RPT6 means six of the eight. A take has no generator settings to rebuild it from afterwards, so collapsing one would lose it. What the lights mean Surface What it says Group A–H hue is the channel, brightness is its level, dark means it is not sounding — while ARM is held it shows who survives a drop instead Mode buttons exactly one lit, always — it cannot disagree with the display F1–F8 lit while that channel is muted — in CONTROL, lit while that column's switch is off its first position , and dark where there is no switch PLAY lit while anything is running REC lit only when a take is actually possible — dark in STEP mode and while MOD is active GRID lit always, and blinking while the selected channel is on an overridden kind NOTE REPEAT lit only while the selected channel behaves as a voice SWING lit while MOD is held or latched TEMPO lit while it is held, and only then — it does not latch SELECT dark until a macro is armed — then one flash per bar while it counts down, steady through the bar it lands on NAVIGATE never lights. Hold it to see the phrase on the pads Arrows, ERASE, SHIFT lit whenever the instrument is running — they always do the same thing The buttons, one by one NOTE REPEAT — the register undo. On a voice, it gives back the previous Turing line: it restores the earlier registers — both of them, so the rhythm cannot move out from under a line you just recovered — forces MELODY and RHYTHM to 0 so it holds, and rewrites immediately. It walks back up to four registers, which is roughly two wraps of human reaction time — the window in which a mutation steals a phrase before your hand arrives. It does nothing on a euclidean channel, which is why it is unlit there. DUPLICATE does nothing. The register undo used to live here and moved to NOTE REPEAT, beside the big encoder with the other master controls. TEMPO — hold it and every encoder turns twice as fast. The knobs are deliberately fine, so that a value can be crept up on rather than jumped over. TEMPO is how you cross a range in a hurry: hold it to get near, let go to land. It changes nothing but speed, it does not latch, and it does not set the tempo — that lives on the touchscreen. SHIFT + GRID switches the selected channel's kind — see Sound and presets . A bare GRID press does nothing, deliberately. MOD + ERASE + ALL clears every modulator at once, returning each value to the base you set — see Modulation . The two buttons beside the big encoder step the selected channel's sound, and which sound depends on the engine: previous or next sample on a drum engine, previous or next preset on a synth engine. Hold SHIFT and they step the kit instead , on a drum engine only. Mute, solo and erase F1–F8 mute channels A–H , regardless of which channel is selected — F3 always mutes CLAP. Tap and it latches; hold past a quarter of a second and it is momentary, back on release. Same button, both gestures: momentary is how you play a gesture, latched is how you make a decision. The mute is on the mixer strip rather than the sequencer track , which is why it survives a snapshot, shows on the touchscreen mixer, and takes the channel's reverb and delay tail with it. CONTROL is the one exception: there the F row carries the page's switches — a plugin's filter type, waveform or section on/off, one button per column, directly above the knob it belongs to. See Deep parameter control . Hold SHIFT and F1–F8 mute again inside CONTROL , and SOLO + F still solos there as everywhere else. SOLO works the same two ways. ERASE + a Group button silences that channel — or, on a channel you have recorded onto, hands the pattern back to the generator. Transport Play starts or stops all eight channels together. The decision is taken once and applied to all eight, so they cannot drift into opposite states. Restart jumps every playhead to step 0 without stopping — for pulling channels back onto the one after a length change has phased them apart. Press Play once after loading a snapshot: loop mode is re-asserted on every transport start, and a fresh load is the one moment it may need it. When it goes quiet Work down this list before suspecting the rig. Most of it is things you did. Check What it looks like Is the tab dashed? the channel is muted, or its generator is silent HITS on a drum 0 hits is a silent channel, not a broken one CHANCE at 0 on a drum, no steps left on a voice nothing fires Is something soloed? every non-soloed Group button goes dark MASTER on the ALL page the global level, easy to leave down Did a drop run? it mutes every channel you did not nominate; F1–F8 lift a mute by hand GATE at its floor on a voice a slow-attack patch never gets far enough to sound A voice that is locked is not silent — LOCK freezes the pattern, it does not mute it. If a whole channel is dead while its tab looks healthy, the fault is below the instrument: see Internals for how the chain is wired, and Manual installation for the checks that catch a stale MIDI route. See also Generating patterns — what HITS, CHANCE, MELODY and RHYTHM actually do Playing and recording — the pad colours in full Modulation — what the ~ and the dashed bar mean

title: What could come next

headings.text: The theme: things that land on the beat

body: What could come next Thirty-eight ideas for this instrument, ranked. None of them is built, and none of them is promised. Ten entries left this page on 2026-08-20 , which is what the gaps in the numbering are: FREEZE, half and double time, BREAK, the ratchet ramp, phrase-locked modulation, audio capture, the pending page, the mute grid, the master-bus insert and beat repeat are all in the guide proper now. What this page is Everything else in this guide describes an instrument you can play today. This page is the opposite: it is the idea list, kept in the open so that anyone forking the project can see what has been considered and how expensive it looked. The list was assembled by reading the code rather than by wishing — every entry has a known mechanism behind it, and several were rejected as impossible before they reached this page. What survives is ordered by impact divided by cost . Cost is S, M or L. S means a day or less and nothing new underneath. M means new state or a new part of the surface, still inside the shape the instrument already has. L means a new mechanism, a new page of the surface, or a question that cannot be answered without measuring the hardware first. Impact is 1 to 5, and it means musical consequence — how much the thing you hear changes — not how clever the idea is. A ratio is where an argument starts, not where it ends. It knows nothing about what depends on what: the countdown ruler sat at rank 22 while nine of the entries above it could not exist without it, which is why it was the first thing built. The numbers are the original ranking positions and they do not shuffle up. A gap in them is an idea that has left this page for the rest of the guide. The theme: things that land on the beat Most of this round answers one request — buildups and drops that are fired by a gesture and then resolve somewhere musical, four or eight or sixteen bars later, instead of happening the instant your finger moves. That rested on something the instrument did not have: it did not know what bar it was on. Its sense of time was a free-running clock scaled by tempo — accurate enough for a sweep, not accurate enough to land a drop. It has one now. The bar count, the arming gesture and its first three payloads are built and written up: the phrase clock and ARM , DROP , the CHANCE ramp and RISE . So have lengths that do not agree , which were on this list and turned out to be reachable already. What is left below is what fires into that clock. Nearly free — ranks 6 to 21 Small work, and in several cases the machinery is already running and has simply never been asked for this. # Idea What it does Cost Impact 9 One knob for how much everything moves The big encoder scales the depth of every live modulator at once, from still to churning. S 4 10 Tempo ramp Six BPM over eight bars into the drop, then hold or snap back. S 4 12 Auto-pilot Arm a build and drop to repeat on a sixteen or thirty-two bar cycle, and the instrument plays its own arrangement while you work on a sound. S 4 15 One-shot fills A second pattern per channel, fired by a pad, played once, returning to the loop by itself. S 4 16 Sound changes land on the bar A kit or preset change waits for the downbeat instead of arriving mid-beat, so sweeping through sounds stops leaving a seam. S 3 18 Gate collapse Every note shortens across the last two bars — tighter and drier without touching a filter — then returns. S 3 19 Velocity swell The pattern leans harder across a build and settles after the drop. S 3 20 The DIN MIDI sockets The Maschine has five-pin MIDI in and out on the back. They work, and this instrument has never used them. Not a build — a switch nobody flipped. S 3 21 Rotate a melody Drums can be spun around the bar; voices cannot. This gives them the same gesture. S 3 Worth the work — ranks 23 to 38 Real work, and the payoff is proportional. Every entry here that queues something onto a downbeat now has the countdown ruler to queue it with. # Idea What it does Cost Impact 26 The build ladder One number from 0 to 100 that moves hits, density, odds, ratchet and cutoff together. Turn it by hand, or arm it and let it climb over sixteen bars. M 5 27 Count-in Once a drop is armed, the last bar clicks, so you can play into it instead of counting. S 2 28 TURN The bar before any landing becomes a fill, and the original pattern comes straight back. Every build ends on a turnaround. M 4 29 BRAKE Hold a button and the tempo bends down; release and it returns at the next bar. A tape-stop that resolves. M 4 30 Punch-in A take that starts on the next bar and stops itself after N bars, so both hands stay on the pads. M 4 31 Timed transpose Up a fifth for eight bars, and back, with the return already paid for. M 4 32 Risers and impacts A sample scheduled backwards from the boundary so its tail lands on the drop. The player for it is already running and idle. M 4 33 Mixer scenes A whole mixer picture — levels, pans, mutes — recalled at the next bar. Two or three make verse, chorus and drop. M 4 34 Banks as scenes The sequencer has sixty-four banks and the instrument uses one. Each is a complete eight-channel pattern set, and they are all already in the snapshot. M 4 35 An undo ring Reroll, randomise and length each destroy a bar with no way back. This keeps the last few and lets you step back through them. M 4 36 Note repeat Hold a pad and it retriggers at a chosen rate. The Maschine gesture this instrument does not have. M 4 37 A chord walker The three voices share a root and a scale, and a slow walker moves the root every few bars, so three unrelated lines become a progression. M 4 38 A drum rhythm register The soft randomiser: drums get the same evolving generator the voices already have. M 4 The big ones — ranks 39 to 54 Each of these needs something the instrument does not have yet: a new page of the surface, a new sense of time, or a measurement before it can even be costed honestly. Two of them may turn out to be impossible on this hardware, and that is stated rather than discovered later. # Idea What it does Cost Impact 39 Lock snapshots and morph Store the whole state of the instrument to a pad; recall it instantly, or morph into it over sixteen bars with every continuous value gliding. L 5 40 Loop roll Hold a button and the channel loops the last eight, four, two or one steps around the playhead, then rejoins. Needs a timing answer this instrument does not have yet. L 5 41 A phrase, not a bar A channel plays four bars where the fourth differs — a real fill in the timeline rather than a swap. L 5 42 An automation lane Per-step automation stored inside the pattern itself: saved with the snapshot, played by the audio engine, immune to any stutter in the driver. L 5 43 Retrograde The bar plays backwards for N bars and then unmirrors. M 3 44 Choke groups Closed hat kills open hat. May be impossible on the drum sampler , whose one-shots play to the end regardless — that has to be measured before it is designed. M 3 45 Duplicate a channel Copy a channel onto another group, pattern and settings and modulation, then let it diverge. M 3 46 Accent and micro-timing A velocity accent mask and a small timing nudge per channel: the weight that swing alone does not give. M 3 47 Sidechain pump The bar-synced gain movement that glues a techno mix. The cheap version is a pump; a true per-kick duck is a different and more expensive feature. M 3 48 A different lead synth Surge XT in place of the current lead engine, with its own parameter tables. M 3 49 The screens draw the curve The pads say how fast a modulator moves; the screens should say what shape it is. M 3 50 A character insert A second effect slot per channel, for drive and colour rather than space. M 3 51 Spare chains A channel becomes a real synth rather than borrowing one, with somewhere to put it. L 4 52 A different drum engine Replacing the sampler with one that has a filter per drum — the only route to per-channel drum timbre that measurement has left open. L 4 53 Layout presets Rearranging which knob sits where, saved per player. M 2 54 Three focuses collapsed into one A simplification of how the instrument decides what a knob is pointed at. The only entry on the list that would cost relearning. M 2 What the list says Four of the top five cost a day or less. The most valuable single idea on the page — a sweep that runs once and lands on the downbeat — is a flag in a data structure that has been shipping since August 2026, because the modulation engine was built to repeat and was never asked to stop. The cheapest genuinely new sound is the odds ramp, because per-step probability is read live while the pattern plays and costs nothing to change. A whole breakdown is one existing control, called once a bar. The four expensive ones are expensive for the same reason, and it is not the code: each needs a new page of the surface or a new answer about timing. On an instrument with sixteen pads and two small screens, where to put a thing is usually harder than how to build it. And two entries are honest unknowns. Whether a sampled drum can be cut off at all, and whether the driver's heartbeat is fast enough to roll a single step, are both questions for the hardware. This project has learned twice that a feature written from the code rather than from the rig is a feature that gets published wrong.
